articles.title_zh: Why China is likely to be cautious about recent Trump-Putin diesel deal

The US may still try to target major buyers of Russian energy despite the deal aimed at cutting American fuel prices, analysts warn
China is likely to view the latest US dealings with Russia as “transactional”, according to observers, who said Beijing was likely to wait and see what the longer-term impact would be given the possibility that Donald Trump might abruptly change course again.
He wrote on social media that another 500,000 tonnes would follow in November, with a further 1 million tonnes “within a short period of time”.
“Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” Trump added.

articles.title_orig: NMPF’s Gregg Doud: Managed China Trade Deal Better for Dairy Than Free Market ‘Chaos’
articles.title_zh: NMPF’s Gregg Doud: Managed China Trade Deal Better for Dairy Than Free Market ‘Chaos’
articles.content_orig:
Agreement, praised on both sides, features controls on Chinese EV shipments and tariff reductions, helping to cool tensions – for now
Weeks of high-wire negotiations between China and the EU culminated in a surprise trade deal that will, among other measures, impose strict quotas on Chinese hybrid car exports to the bloc and slash Chinese tariffs on a variety of European goods.
China’s Ministry of Commerce described the deal as an “upward arrangement” based on the country’s outbound shipments of hybrid cars in 2025, adding the agreement would ensure further room for the “stable growth” of Chinese companies’ exports.

articles.title_orig: Alexander Zverev to end year as world number one after Carlos Alacaraz loses
articles.title_zh: Alexander Zverev to end year as world number one after Carlos Alacaraz loses
articles.content_orig:
By TOM LAWRENCE, NEWS REPORTER
Updated: 06:00 EDT, 12 October 2026
Britain is losing pubs at a rate of around one a day – with more than 5,000 job losses expected by the end of the year.
Almost 300 businesses permanently closed their doors in the first nine months of the year, according to the British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA).
Pub operators blamed the latest round of closures on Labour's sky-high tax burden alongside regulatory costs in the sector.
Andy Burnham has promised to cut business rates by 20 per cent for pubs in England from next year, in a bid to relieve business owners.
However, the move may come too late for around 200 pubs if the current trend of closures continues.
As a new budget looms, landlords will nervously await news of any tax rises which could compound their misery.
New data from the BBPA showed that 295 British pubs shut their doors by the end of September since the start of the year.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham pictured at the Hare pub in Harlow, Essex
England saw 226 pubs close in total over the period, while 64 shut their doors in Scotland and five closed in Wales.
Within England, the South East and North West saw particularly high levels of closures, with 42 and 39 closures respectively.
The trade body estimated that around 360 pubs will permanently shut their doors by the end of the year.
This would result in around 5,000 job losses, with more than half of these roles being filled by under-25s, the BBPA said.
The pub sector has benefited from a 15 per cent discount to business rates for the current tax year, with a 20 per cent cut from next year.
Trade industry bosses said recent support will be a significant help but urged the Prime Minister to tackle other taxes and labour costs affecting business.
Despite some respite from the new Prime Minister, pubs are still recovering from the devastation caused by Rachel Reeves's tax bomb budget in 2025.
The then-chancellor added £322 million of business costs for pubs and breweries, leaving hundreds across the country to cut staff, raise prices or close their doors.
It also caused a dent in the pockets of punters, as the price of a pint soared above £10 in London for the first time.
Pub owners across the country will nervously await Chancellor John Heealy's upcoming budget
Emma McClarkin, chief executive of the BBPA, said: 'When a local closes, the damage is felt far and wide.
'It's not just workers, communities, our heritage and high streets who lose out when a pub closes – the Treasury loses, on average, £200,000 in tax receipts every time a local calls last orders.
'The Prime Minister has pledged that the cavalry is coming, which is why we're asking Government to tackle the root of the problem through a permanently fair and sustainable rates burden, freezing beer duty, increasing draught relief and reviewing employment costs for under-25s.
'This will mean we can carry on keeping people in jobs, boosting the economy, and being at the heart of communities.'
Do YOU have a story? E-mail tom.lawrence@dailymail.co.uk

articles.title_orig: World, religious leaders unite in prayer for Pope Leo, praising his ‘profound serenity and transparency’
articles.title_zh: World, religious leaders unite in prayer for Pope Leo, praising his ‘profound serenity and transparency’
articles.content_orig:
(OSV News) — Prominent political and religious leaders from around the world expressed well wishes and prayers for Pope Leo XIV after he announced he would undergo surgery to remove a lung nodule.
The pope made the surprise announcement while addressing pilgrims Oct. 11 during his Sunday Angelus address.
After doctors detected “a small, localized nodule” in his lung, Pope Leo said he would follow their advice and “undergo surgery to remove it.”
“The operation is already scheduled to take place in the coming days,” he said. ” I thank you for your spiritual closeness and entrust myself to your prayers.”
Not long after his announcement, Italian President Sergio Mattarella published a letter to Pope Leo saying that the news of his surgery “was received with deep empathy and emotion by all the Italian people.”
“In view of your hospitalization in the coming days, may the affectionate thoughts of all Italians reach you, which I convey while adding my own personal sentiments,” Mattarella wrote. “The Italian people stand close to you.”
The Italian head of state said the pope could count on the prayers of not only the Catholic faithful, but also “on the caring thoughts of countless people, in Italy as well as across the world, whether believers or non-believers.”
Several world leaders also took to X to send well wishes to the pope, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who wished Pope Leo “a successful surgery and a swift, full recovery.”
“Our thoughts and prayers are with him, and we hope he will soon be back in good health and strength,” Zelenskyy wrote. “Ukraine is deeply grateful to His Holiness for his prayers and his strong, consistent calls for a dignified and durable peace.”
In a brief message posted to X, Israeli President Isaac Herzog wrote: “From the holy city of Jerusalem, I wish Pope Leo XIV a full and speedy recovery.”
Maltese Prime Minister Robert Abela also extended “prayers and best wishes” to the pope for “a successful procedure and a complete recovery.”
Pope Leo also received prayers from Anglican Archbishop Sarah Mullaly of Canterbury, who said she was “holding Pope Leo XIV in my prayers over these coming days, asking for God’s protection, closeness and care.”
“With Christians across the country and around the world, I pray for the pope’s swift recovery,” the head of the Church of England wrote on X.
Viktor Eichner, the World Jewish Congress’ representative to the Holy See, also posted on X, writing: “On behalf of the World Jewish Congress, I wish Pope Leo XIV a successful surgery and a speedy recovery. May he return to full strength soon.”
The surgery announcement came as Pope Leo prepares to embark on his longest international trip to date: a 12-day apostolic visit to Latin America, including stops in Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru.
At the Angelus, the pope greeted a group of Peruvian pilgrims and thanked them for praying for his upcoming visit, indicating the trip was still moving forward.
At a press conference in Uruguay, the first stop in the pope’s Nov. 6-17 apostolic trip, Cardinal Daniel Sturla of Montevideo told journalists Oct. 11 that although the announcement “was a surprise,” the pope’s greetings to the Peruvian pilgrims showed that “the plans remain the same.”
“Obviously, we are all praying for the pope’s health and trust that everything will go well, that he will recover and be able to be here on the scheduled date,” Cardinal Sturla said.
When asked if any precautions will be taken given that the pope is expected to arrive in less than a month, the Uruguayan cardinal said he believed so and that the pope “always travels accompanied by his personal physician and other healthcare staff.”
“I understand that some care will need to be taken,” Cardinal Sturla said. “We will be instructed in the coming days. We will be very attentive to that, but confident that everything will go well and that we are moving forward.”
Argentine President Javier Milei extended his “affection and best wishes” ahead of the pope’s surgery. Pope Leo will visit Argentina Nov. 8-11.
“All of Argentina accompanies His Holiness with affection and prayer, wishing him a prompt and full recovery,” Milei wrote on X. “From our country, we join in prayer for his health, in the hope that he may soon continue guiding the Church with his characteristic wisdom and strength.”
The Argentine bishops’ conference issued a statement calling on the country’s Catholics to pray for Pope Leo ahead of his surgery.
“We ask the Lord to grant him strength and peace at this time, that the surgery proceeds favorably, and that he may achieve a prompt and full recovery,” the bishops wrote.
Noting the pope’s “serenity and confidence” in his announcement, the bishops urged Catholics to “remain spiritually united with him.”
In Peru, where Pope Leo is scheduled to visit Nov. 11-17, President Keiko Fujimori took to X to express her and her country’s “profound affection and solidarity” with the pope “in the face of this health issue, which we hope he will overcome fully and successfully.”
“Our hearts and our prayers are with him, in the hope of soon having him among us,” Fujimori wrote. “With deep faith and hope, we pray that the Holy Father has a prompt recovery and may continue guiding, with wisdom and strength, the path of faith of the entire Holy Church.”
In a statement released shortly after the pope’s announcement, Bishop Carlos Enrique García Camader of Lurin, president of the Peruvian bishops’ conference, noted the pope’s “profound serenity and transparency” in announcing his surgery and that his “testimony of fortitude and humility in sharing this news moves us and immediately calls us to unity in prayer.”
“The Peruvian Episcopate invites all Catholic people and people of goodwill to unite in prayer for the health of His Holiness Pope Leo XIV, raising our supplications to God, Lord of life and source of all health, so that He may strengthen him and grant him the health required for the fulfillment of his mission,” Bishop García wrote.
He also invoked Mary’s intercession “so that in the fullness of his strength he may continue fulfilling his mission in service to the Church and all humanity, continuing to be a messenger of peace and hope, and a witness of unity, fraternity, and encounter among all peoples.”
Junno Arocho Esteves is an international correspondent for OSV News. Follow him on X @jae_journalist

articles.title_orig: China’s Growth Machine
articles.title_zh: China’s Growth Machine
articles.content_orig:
Imagine if Y Combinator owned and ran San Francisco. Too much traffic? That’s bad for business. Highway 101 would be triple- or quadruple-deckered, and the metropolitan area might have a dozen subway lines, more like Madrid’s or Osaka’s networks than the BART as it stands. Heritage buildings? They’re nice, but this is a tech town. Skyscrapers would fill the entire peninsula. Instead of wealth taxes on billionaires, the city might even cut taxes to encourage more founders and companies to move there.
This is only a slight caricature of how city government works in China. Provincial cities like Hefei and Hangzhou have become world-leading centers of commerce in electric vehicles, consumer electronics, solar panels, batteries, and AI, steered by mayors whose career incentives are similar to those of partners in a venture capital firm, getting promoted if their portfolio grows and fired if it fails. The cities they run function as vertically integrated conglomerates that benefit not just from the success of their local champions, but also from the broader growth generated by masses of companies in their slipstream.
In the West, China’s success is often attributed to the central government’s willingness to pick winners and direct its economy from above. Many Westerners have concluded that a similar top-down approach is needed in their countries to create champions that can compete with China’s. But Beijing’s role is more akin to being a rulemaker in a great tournament. Subnational governments – provinces, cities, towns, villages – are responsible for around 85 percent of public expenditure, according to the IMF, the lion’s share of which is spent at city level. 1
The heavy state involvement correctly perceived by observers belongs not to Beijing but to those local governments, of which China has thousands, and which compete with one another for investment and prestige. These local growth machines and the competition between them are what drives China’s stunning economic success, and what the Western world must embrace to keep up.
For the initial decades after China’s economic opening in the 1980s, ‘Made in China’ meant cheap goods mass-produced for Western businesses. Today, Chinese companies lead the world in high-tech manufacturing, and many of them are household names in the West. Huawei is arguably the world’s most advanced telecoms company; BYD is the largest electric automaker; and DJI makes over 90 percent of consumer drones. Less familiar but no less important are companies like Geely, an auto giant which began in the 1980s as a refrigerator parts manufacturer and now owns Volvo, Lotus, Polestar and a stake in Aston Martin; and Vivo, now India’s biggest smartphone supplier.
What all have in common is that Beijing played no role in their creation. They were private companies encouraged by local governments. Huawei, BYD, and DJI emerged from Shenzhen’s Special Economic Zone, where municipal bureaucrats could write local regulations without regard for national rules. Geely was quietly supported by Zhejiang province at a time when only state-designated automakers were meant to build cars. Vivo spun off from a company founded in Dongguan, after Zhongshan, the neighboring city, wouldn’t give the company leaders equity.
Some sectors, such as batteries, electronics, and most recently electric vehicles, have received special support from Beijing as strategic industries. Companies in these areas benefited from subsidies, tax rebates, and in the case of electric cars, sales tax exemptions. But though the state was happy to lend its support to certain sectors, it was agnostic as to which specific firms and regions rose to dominance by means of that support. Beijing set a prize, and local bureaucrats competed to win it.
Hefei, the capital of Anhui province in inland Eastern China, is the most famous illustration of this process in action. In 2008, the municipal government invested $500 million in the electronic display company BOE Technology to build a new-generation LCD production line, bringing China to the cutting edge of panel production for the first time. At the time, Hefei was an unremarkable city with no display industry, and BOE was only the world’s ninth-largest manufacturer of LCD displays. The city provided the necessary land, utility connections, and cheap capital (investing almost a tenth of its total revenue that year) to set up a subsidiary company with BOE, in which it had an 81 percent stake. The bet paid off. BOE is now the world’s largest display panel manufacturer and makes about a quarter of smartphone screens worldwide.
The city reinvested the returns from its investment in other venture capital–like bets, which have won big surprisingly often. Hefei’s investment in carmaker NIO, which the city backed in 2020 in exchange for a 24 percent stake, paid off with an internal rate of return exceeding 30 percent. CXMT (Changxin Memory Technologies), 24 percent of which is directly or indirectly owned by the city of Hefei, runs just behind Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron with 7 percent of the global market for DRAM chips, the short-term memory used in smartphones, PCs, and data centers. Over the decade to 2023, the city had invested roughly $25 billion of public funds, generating reported earnings of nearly $9 billion.
Other cities have followed the venture capital model to bring in similar growth in jobs and tax revenues. The city of Wuhu imported a secondhand Ford engine line from Britain, lured engineers away from state behemoth FAW (First Automotive Works), and copied a Volkswagen design to build a local carmaker. That makeshift venture eventually grew into Chery, today one of the country’s leading carmakers and supplier of Britain’s bestselling car in March 2026, the Jaecoo 7. As well as having seen growth in jobs, exports, and tax revenues, the city of Wuhu retains a 21 percent stake in Chery, worth around $3.7 billion.
Ningde, a relatively modest city in Fujian province in the southeast, is the founding site of CATL, now the world’s biggest battery producer. The city’s leaders made a strategic wager from its founding in 2011, committing land, infrastructure, tax support, administrative coordination, and supplier attraction efforts to help the still-young battery company to scale. CATL’s bases in Ningde now have capacity to produce 330 gigawatt hours of batteries per year – equivalent to almost half the global demand for electric vehicle batteries in 2023.
China’s mayors and provincial governors turn their cities into venture capital portfolios because of the system of incentives in which they operate. 2 Each cadre (the party members and other officials who run the Chinese state) is scored by their superiors in a secret file built up over the course of their career. Prefecture-level party secretaries evaluate county chiefs, who in turn evaluate their juniors heading up townships, who evaluate village leaders, down to the lowest party member.
Promotions – not just for politicians, but across the civil service – are based in large part on scoring the economic performance of the province or city that a cadre is responsible for. For example, the Shaoxing Municipal Party Committee’s 2008 assessment for city leaders featured 100 base points, of which 54 were awarded for economic development , including growth in GDP per capita, local revenue, industrial investment, and exports. Across China in the 2000s, officials who presided over growth 3.3 percentage points higher than their predecessors were 40 to 50 percent more likely to be promoted. Whereas success leads to promotion, failure can mean early retirement, demotion, or disciplinary action.
To further incentivize bureaucrats, promotions are governed by strict, albeit not explicit, age ceilings . A cadre must make the jump from county officialdom to prefecture level by their mid-forties, must take the next jump to provincial or ministerial level by their mid-fifties, and is unlikely ever to rea

articles.title_orig: World’s Energy Order Tested Again as Iran War’s Reach Extends Further
articles.title_zh: World’s Energy Order Tested Again as Iran War’s Reach Extends Further
articles.content_orig:
A major energy conference is going ahead in Riyadh from Sunday despite a Houthi attack on the city’s King Khalid International Airport that killed 12 people and injured 309, according to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation.
Saudi ⁠Arabia’s Ministry of Energy said on Sunday that the 25th ⁠World Petroleum Council Energy Congress has begun ‌in Riyadh. The 17th International Energy Forum (IEF) Ministerial will be held on the sidelines of the conference, called Riyadh Energy Week, which is to run until Thursday.
But Italy, the cohost of the IEF, will join the meeting via videolink. Nigeria, the other cohost, is sending a representative to the event.
The IEF brings together 68 countries that account for more than 90 percent of global oil and gas supplies and demand. Its members include Saudi Arabia, the United States and Russia. The meeting comes as the US-Israel war on Iran has disrupted energy flows and pushed governments to reassess their energy security.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera looks at where the world’s energy comes from, how much is produced in the Middle East and which countries have strategic reserves to fall back on.
Energy heats our homes, fuels our cars, keeps the lights on and runs the factories that make what we buy. It comes from fossil fuels such as oil, coal and gas as well as nuclear power and renewables.
Despite rapid growth in renewables, fossil fuels still account for nearly 81 percent of global energy consumption. Oil is the largest source at 31.4 percent, followed by coal at 25.9 percent and natural gas at 23.5 percent. Traditional biomass, nuclear power and other sources make up the rest.
Production is concentrated in a handful of regions, so disruptions in any of them ripple through global markets.
The Middle East is the largest oil-producing region, and North America is the largest natural gas producer. Russia and Central Asia are also major producers of both.
The Middle East’s importance to energy markets is also about geography. Three narrow waterways connect its producers with consumers around the world.
Before the Iran war, about 27 percent of global seaborne oil trade and almost 20 percent of liquefied natural gas trade transited through the Strait of Hormuz on the eastern side of the Arabian Peninsula.
On the peninsula’s western side, the Bab al-Mandeb strait links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, and the Suez Canal connects the Red Sea with the Mediterranean. As the Iran war has spilled over into other areas of the Middle East and Yemen’s civil war has ramped up, traffic has been reduced through both the strait and canal, forcing some energy shipments on longer routes around Africa.
“That’s probably the first time we’ve really seen a major constriction of a chokepoint,” said Richard Matthews, director of consultancy and research at Gibson Shipbrokers, a London-based shipbroking and maritime advisory service.
He told Al Jazeera that what makes the Strait of Hormuz different from other chokepoints is “there is no alternative maritime route. There are some pipelines, but there’s no alternative, which is why it’s been so significant in terms of cargo volume.”
Gulf ports are where much of the region’s energy begins its journey to the rest of the world.
Further down the supply chain, people and businesses are feeling the disruption through the rising cost of essentials.
Countries that rely on oil, gas and fertiliser from the Gulf face higher prices, longer waits for shipments and the need to find other suppliers. Even where deals have kept goods moving, the extra costs are being passed down the chain.
Eritrea and Madagascar are the most dependent on Middle Eastern oil, each sourcing about 90 percent of their supply from the region. They are followed by Pakistan (78 percent), Japan (77 percent) and Kenya (77 percent).
Gas has been even harder to replace than oil because most of it travels as liquefied natural gas from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates through the Strait of Hormuz.
Countries that depend on these shipments are paying more for fuel and electricity and competing for a smaller pool of cargoes. Poorer importers with little storage have struggled the most to find alternatives.
The countries that rely most heavily on Middle Eastern gas are mostly in Asia. South Korea sources 31 percent of the gas it uses from the region, followed by India (29 percent), Pakistan (27 percent) and Taiwan (26 percent).
Countries keep emergency oil stocks for when supplies are cut off or reduced, and these have been the world’s main cushion during the war. That cushion is now wearing thin.
Western countries have little left to release, energy industry leaders warned, and the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve is at its lowest level since 1982.
“Estimates suggest less than 6 billion barrels of commercial inventories remain today with the vast majority not practically available,” Amin Nasser, head of Saudi Aramco, told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London on Monday.
The International Energy Agency, which coordinates emergency stocks for its members, released a record 400 million barrels of oil in March. It is now preparing to release another 100 million barrels of crude and diesel to ease soaring diesel prices although some of this may be oil from the March release that has yet to reach the market.
A storm in the Gulf of Mexico and attacks in Saudi Arabia are now threatening supplies again, keeping oil prices above $100 a barrel.
Before this year’s releases, China held by far the largest reserves, an estimated 1.4 billion barrels, more than the rest of the list combined. The US was second with 413 million barrels, followed by Japan with 263 million.

articles.title_orig: EU and China agree to moderate Chinese hybrid vehicle exports
articles.title_zh: EU and China agree to moderate Chinese hybrid vehicle exports
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The European Union (EU) and China have agreed a shared understanding to moderate Chinese exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to the EU, Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said in Beijing.
He said the arrangement opens the prospect of reducing those exports by more than half.
A document seen by Bloomberg indicates that the EU would limit imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles to 350,000 cars a year.
The safeguard measure could take effect as soon as 1 December.
The ceiling would increase by 6% annually from the second year and run for four years, during which both sides would commit to following World Trade Organization rules.
It would apply to all sources of EU imports, including partners with free-trade agreements.
"It is a crucial first step – but only a first step – in the process of rebalancing," Šefčovič said.
Šefčovič outlined two further understandings. One would widen access to the Chinese market for EU products, ranging from car parts to olive oil and footwear, through lower most-favoured-nation tariffs.
These products have a current export value of almost €4bn ($4.47bn), with duty savings of at least €225m. The other would further ease China's export licensing for rare earths and permanent magnets.
According to the Chinese commerce ministry, as cited in Reuters ' report, Commerce Minister Wang Wentao told Šefčovič that China was not the root cause of the EU's problems but a partner in resolving them.
The EU's trade deficit with China has grown to more than €1bn a day.
In the second quarter of 2026, its goods trade deficit with China stood at €103bn, the highest since the third quarter of 2022.
Šefčovič said EU president von der Leyen will review the outcomes with leaders at the European Council, which will make the final decision.
Reuters reported that EU leaders will meet in Brussels on 15 October to decide whether the result marks the start of rebalancing.
It also said EU governments are alarmed by the sharp rise in car imports from China while European carmakers cut jobs, notably Volkswagen, where 100,000 jobs are going .
Šefčovič and Wang will meet again by January, and the third Trade and Investment Consultations are scheduled for March.
"EU and China agree to moderate Chinese hybrid vehicle exports" was originally created and published by Just Auto , a GlobalData owned brand.

articles.title_orig: Store Responds After Kelly Clarkson Says Staff Treated Her Like Julia Roberts’ ‘Pretty Woman’ Character
articles.title_zh: Store Responds After Kelly Clarkson Says Staff Treated Her Like Julia Roberts’ ‘Pretty Woman’ Character
articles.content_orig:
Treat Yourself to ‘Little Luxuries’ In Our Newest Box — for 73% Off
Brooklyn specialty shop Art of Play has responded after singer Kelly Clarkson accused the store of treating her “like Julia Roberts character in Pretty Woman.”
Art of Play posted a statement on its Instagram page after Clarkson tweeted on Oct. 10 that she visited the store, with her eye on a few items but instead was “looked at as if I couldn’t afford it.”
Clarkson added that she “was told he could find something comparable for me.”
“Wow, dude. You’re an idiot and just lost a huge sale,” Clarkson wrote on X, before naming the New York City store.
The small business responded on Oct. 11, saying in a statement that Clarkson had attempted to buy a permanent installation that is not for sale.
“Yesterday, Kelly Clarkson visited us in Brooklyn and inquired about buying ‘Molly,’ a one-of-a-kind singing and dancing bird automaton who plays an important role in the magic shows we host here,” the store wrote on its social media page. “Molly is permanently attached to the wall and isn’t for sale. However, the negative experience Kelly described on twitter would resonate with anyone who has ever felt judged in a shop.”
The store, which wrote that it had become the subject of backlash after Clarkson’s post, thanked those who supported it.
“Thanks to all our friends for their support and welcome to all the curious folks who have discovered us amidst the drama,” Art of Play wrote in the statement, before referencing Clarkson’s hit song. “We’re going to keep our heads down and hopefully, we can clear things up with Kelly someday. As a talented popular singer once said ‘what doesn’t kill you makes you stronger.’”
Clarkson did not immediately respond to TODAY.com ’s request for comment. But in another post on X, Clarkson challenged the store’s statement, describing the staff as “not only rude, you’re also a liar.”
“Cool, cool. Sure, it wasn’t for sale. That’s the narrative Art of Play is gonna go with 👍” Clarkson wrote on the social media platform Oct. 11.
The singer then continued with her version of events.
“So the whole conversation we had when I asked you if it was for sale whilst pointing to the price tag hanging on the wall with the title Singing Bird didn’t happen as you elevator eyed me saying in a condescending tone ‘yes, it’s for sale but it costs 15,000 dollars so if you’d like me to find something comparable for you I can.’” she wrote in the post, appearing to convey sarcasm. “That all never happened and now it’s not for sale.”
The singer also hit back at criticisms that she doesn’t support small businesses.
“You don’t get a free pass to treat people less than in your store just because you are a small business,” she wrote. “It’s not that hard to be kind. I never blast people but you my friend were an exception.”
She concluded by saying, “Your store is really cool.”
“Unfortunately, you aren’t,” she wrote.
Art of Play did not immediately respond to TODAY.com’s request for comment on Clarkson’s Oct. 11 post. The store, however, shared a follow-up post to its Instagram early Oct. 12 in an effort to “clarify one additional detail about Kelly Clarkson’s visit.”
“During the 5 minutes she spent in the store, she inquired about our mechanical bird puppet named Molly,” the Oct. 12 post from Art of Play said. “We explained that while Molly is permanently attached to the wall and serves as a de facto mascot for our shop, a nearly identical automaton is owned by the creator of the machines, a brilliant artist named Bliss Kolb who lives in Seattle. He told us he would be willing to part with Molly’s twin for $15,000.”
The store said employees offered to show her another option for a singing bird that was available to take home that day for $2,000 but Clarkson “did not stick around long enough to see it.”
Art of Play said it reached out to the singer directly to “clear the air.”
Art of Play, which sits in the neighborhood of Brooklyn Heights, is a specialty store that features home goods in addition to magic-themed gifts, cards and games.
In her post, Clarkson said that she “drove all the way to Brooklyn” to take a peek at the store, already with a few things in mind to purchase. She compared her experience to that of Julia Roberts’ “Pretty Woman” character Vivian Ward when she is brushed off by a Beverly Hills salesperson who assumes she can’t afford the expensive items in the store because of her casual appearance.
Art of Play said in the statement that the store invites all shoppers to play with their items.
“And they do, many stay for hours enjoying our puzzles, games and toys,” the store said.
The criticisms they’ve been receiving have taken them by surprise, the store said in the statement.
“Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by 8 million people who have never visited our store,” the statement said. “It’s been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity.”
The bird automaton appears to have not been available for purchase in the past. Several weeks ago, the store had made a post about their “favorite items not for sale,” featuring an image of the bird automaton.
Since the parties’ comments, the internet has been divided with Clarkson’s fans flocking to the store’s pages to express their disappointment. Many others, including New York locals, have been commenting as well, sharing their positive experiences with the shop.
Kimmy Yam is a reporter for NBC Asian America.

articles.title_orig: Starbucks says it is not buying Chipotle after takeover speculation
articles.title_zh: Starbucks says it is not buying Chipotle after takeover speculation
articles.content_orig:
Starbucks on Monday denied that it is considering acquiring Chipotle Mexican Grill in what would be the biggest ever restaurant takeover.
"Starbucks is not buying Chipotle," a Starbucks spokesperson told CNBC's Jim Cramer.
Chipotle's stock was down more than 2% in premarket trading Monday following the denial, while Starbucks shares were more than 1% higher.
The coffee giant's denial comes after days of rumors about a potential mega-deal between the two restaurant companies.
On Thursday, the Financial Times reported that Starbucks has been working with advisers on a takeover proposal of Chipotle in recent months. The newspaper cited people familiar with the matter.
Earlier in October, Semafor reported that Chipotle had hired advisers to defend against activist investors or an unwanted takeover bid. The fast-casual chain is trying to recover from a rocky 2025 , when traffic to its restaurants fell. Chipotle shares are down about 20% over the last year, making it a cheaper target.
The deal rumors sent shares of Chipotle higher, while Starbucks stock fell on the reports.
Chipotle investors were looking forward to a potential reunion with Brian Niccol, who previously led Chipotle and is now CEO of Starbucks. But Starbucks shareholders were largely concerned about an expensive distraction while the coffee chain is in the middle of its own turnaround.

articles.title_orig: The China-EU Trade Truce Buys Time - The Diplomat
articles.title_zh: The China-EU Trade Truce Buys Time - The Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic and Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao shake hands after their talks in Beijing, China, Oct, 9, 2026.
Like last month’s summit between the U.S. and Chinese presidents, the China-EU Trade and Investment Consultations in Beijing were primarily about stabilization rather than a breakthrough. EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic and Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao closed a handful of agreements and confirmed that neither side wants a trade war. However, the structural issues remain unresolved. What both sides gained is time.
For the European Union, the choice is increasingly difficult: secure real concessions from Beijing to address structural trade imbalances or deploy stronger unilateral measures to protect its industrial base. Compounding this dilemma is Europe’s risk of becoming an adjustment variable in the China-U.S. strategic competition , absorbing diverted Chinese exports when tensions escalate while losing market opportunities and negotiating leverage when Washington and Beijing strike bilateral deals. Washington holds the technology lever, while Beijing controls critical minerals and key nodes of global supply chains. Europe depends on both.
The most concrete outcome of the talks concerns the automotive sector. Under a preliminary deal, Chinese exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to the EU could be curbed more than half against projected levels over the next four years. The stakes are high. In 2025, the EU imported more than 1 million Chinese-made cars , worth $15.5 billion (13.7 billion euros) and up 30 percent in volume on 2024. Hybrids tell the story best : 659 Chinese hybrids sold in the EU in 2022, versus more than 160,000 in the first seven months of 2026, plus almost 218,000 plug-in hybrids.
Chinese brands now hold almost 12 percent of Europe’s new-car market , up from 1 percent five years ago, and roughly a third of plug-in hybrid sales. In the United States, Chinese cars are absent. Washington has effectively shut Chinese electric vehicles out of its market through 100 percent tariffs , while Europe remains far more exposed to Chinese automotive imports. The U.S., a market of 16.2 million new vehicles, bought fewer than 90,000 China-made vehicles in 2024, almost all of them Western brands built in China.
The rapid expansion of Chinese carmakers has intensified competitive pressures on European manufacturers, particularly in Germany and France, which had pushed for tougher trade measures. The proposed 50 percent reduction in Chinese hybrid exports is a step forward, but it is measured against projected growth, not current volumes.
China’s hybrid expansion accelerated after the EU imposed tariffs on Chinese battery-electric vehicles in 2024 . Manufacturers shifted toward hybrids, which were exempt from those duties. While Washington imposed steep barriers to Chinese electric vehicles, Brussels left a significant loophole. The hybrid cars deal is therefore less a breakthrough than an attempt to correct a weakness in Europe’s trade policy.
As for whether the deal will work, much will depend on enforcement. Effective restrictions could give European automakers time to adjust. Weak implementation would allow Chinese exports to expand further, forcing Brussels to consider tougher measures and risking retaliation that could disrupt supply chains and investment on both sides. Meanwhile, Chinese automakers are increasingly moving from exports to manufacturing inside Europe . The strategic question is no longer simply how many Chinese cars are imported in the European market, but where industrial value is created, who controls the technology, and where the jobs are located.
The second result concerns market access and trade rebalancing. Brussels and Beijing agreed to cut tariffs on a range of EU products to the most-favored-nation (MFN) rates set under WTO rules. The goods covered, from car parts to olive oil and footwear, account for nearly $4.7 billion in exports. If implemented, the measure would save European exporters at least $260 million in duties.
Set against the trade figures, however, it is a small gain. In her State of the Union speech, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the EU’s deficit with China “unsustainable .” It now runs at more than 1 billion euros a day. The goods deficit rose from 306 billion euros in 2024 to 360 billion euros in 2025 and could reach 400 billion euros ($470 billion) this year, according to Eurostat.
The United States, meanwhile, moved in the opposite direction. In 2025, its goods deficit with China fell by almost a third to $202 billion, the lowest in two decades , as imports from China dropped 30 percent. China’s share of U.S. imports fell to about 9 percent, the lowest since it joined the WTO in 2001. The EU’s goods deficit with China is now twice America’s. What Washington kept out with tariffs, Europe increasingly absorbs.
Sefcovic defended the new deal with China as the result of an intense negotiation, noting that Washington had needed far more rounds to get its own deal. But he warned against complacency.
The third result concerns critical raw materials, above all rare earths and permanent magnets. This is where Europe depends on China most – 98 percent of EU demand for rare earth magnets is met by Chinese imports. Beijing will ease export licensing for European companies through a green channel. That matters for carmakers, renewables, and defense. But Beijing keeps control of the licenses, and with it the power to turn supplies on and off.
Washington got more. At the Busan summit in October 2025 , the United States secured a one-year suspension of China’s new export restrictions and general licenses for its companies. The White House summit in September 2026 extended that suspension until January 10, 2027. Brussels obtained faster procedures for licenses that remain individual and revocable. Washington negotiated with tariffs and semiconductor controls on the table. Europe only trade-defense tools it has yet to use.
The industrial strategies differ as well. The United States has stepped up directly, with the Pentagon taking a stake in MP Materials and Washington forging minerals deals with Australia and Japan. Europe is relying on the Critical Raw Materials Act and RESourceEU , a sound framework but slower and less funded. Faster licenses make Europe’s supplies more predictable, but they do not make it less dependent.
That’s not to say Europe has no leverage. Four days before the talks, France and Germany jointly called for stronger trade defense instruments against Chinese overcapacity, subsidies, and market distortions. Beijing got the message. In response, official Beijing urged Paris and Berlin not to push the EU toward protectionist tools. Germany’s position carried the most weight. The European Commission went to Beijing with more leverage than before.
EU leaders will discuss the deal at the European Council on October 15–16. They will find a difficult balance in it. The hybrid agreement limits Chinese exports that hurt European carmakers. The rare earth agreement eases Chinese exports that the same carmakers rely on. Europe wants fewer of some Chinese goods and a steady supply of others, and on both counts the decision rests with Beijing. The recent truce calms the relationship but leaves the imbalances in place.
What Europe does with the next few months will matter more than the deal itself. If it invests in competitiveness, innovation and economic security, it can negotiate from strength next time. If it doesn’t, it will remain the adjustment variable in a rivalry it does not control.

articles.title_orig: How Ivanka Trump’s Guo Pei dress put Chinese high fashion in spotlight
articles.title_zh: How Ivanka Trump’s Guo Pei dress put Chinese high fashion in spotlight
articles.content_orig:
Guo, one of China’s best-known couturiers, has also designed outfits for celebrities including pop star Rihanna
Ivanka Trump’s appearance in a blue embroidered couture outfit during the welcome ceremony for President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington last month has drawn attention to its designer and the growing international profile of Chinese bespoke fashion.
The outfit was designed by Guo Pei, one of China’s best-known couturiers, who also created the spectacular yellow embroidered cape with a long train and fur trim worn by pop star Rihanna at the 2015 Met Gala.
Guo told the South China Morning Post that Trump’s outfit was not created specifically for the diplomatic occasion, but its design and colour were carefully considered. She said blue was chosen to convey calm and a shared aspiration for peace.
The outfit was originally intended for a trip to China that US President Donald Trump’s eldest daughter had expected to make with her father. Guo said she and Ivanka Trump discussed its design and colour at the beginning of the year.

articles.title_orig: Google announces $179 Fitbit Edge tracker with display, GPS
articles.title_zh: Google announces $179 Fitbit Edge tracker with display, GPS
articles.content_orig:
Google is following the Fitbit Air launched in May with a second tracker that features a screen called the Fitbit Edge.
The Fitbit Edge features a wide, pill-shaped AMOLED screen — protected by Gorilla Glass 3 — that offers 46% more display than the Charge 6 from 2023. The 11.5mm-thick body is made from precision-crafted aluminum with nano-molding technology to allow for a 40% more precise GPS (versus Charge 6), while there’s a dedicated altimeter for elevation tracking. On the right side, you’ll find a large button for tactile control, like when swimming. This device has IP68 / 5ATM dust and water protection.
On the underside, you’ll find the sensors. The Fitbit Edge has an accelerometer, altimeter, ambient light sensor, far-field skin temperature sensor, gyroscope, heart rate sensor, multipurpose electrical sensors (ECG), and red and infrared sensors (SpO2).
The Fitbit Edge uses the same magnetic USB-C charger as the Fitbit Air. A 5-minute charge gives you a day of battery, while a full top-up takes 90 minutes. Battery life is rated at a week with the always-on display disabled. When enabled, the Fitbit Edge comes in at around 2 days. Like the Pixel Watch 5, you can open the device to replace the battery.
The Fitbit Edge is available in the following colors:
The bands are replaceable with a new swap mechanism and four additional designs:
Supporting Android and iOS, the Edge is running a Fitbit operating system similar to the Air. A larger screen unlocks a richer interface that takes inspiration from the Pixel Watch 5.
Google showed a dozen or so watch faces for the Fitbit Edge with analog and digital options. You can customize what complications appear via the Google Health app.
Swiping left/right from the watch face lets you access various tiles, with the order customizable. This includes Quick start (for different exercises), Focus metrics, Sleep, Heart, Cycle health, Weather, Timers, Alarms, and Music controls.
Compared to the Charge 6, music controls work with any app on your paired device, while phone notifications are also available. Quick replies to messages are limited to Android due to iOS platform limitations. You also get Google Maps navigation, but there is no Google Wallet given the lack of NFC.
The Exercise app lets you track over 50 types of activity with real-time guidance and workout views. The Fitbit Edge can connect to equipment with heart rate broadcasting.
The Fitbit Edge (and the Air) feature upgraded automatic activity detection. This AI-powered contextual reasoning can learn your habits over time to add support for over 100 activities.
You can have the Fitbit Air, Edge, and Pixel Watch 5 operate on the same account with seamless switching.
The Fitbit Edge costs $179.99 with pre-orders open today and availability on October 27. A Stephen Curry Special Edition is available for $219.99 with a custom band.

articles.title_orig: Kailua Village is named 2026 IFEA World Festival & Event City
articles.title_zh: Kailua Village is named 2026 IFEA World Festival & Event City
articles.content_orig:
Privacy Policy | About Our Ads
The International Festivals & Events Association honored Kailua Village during  the 71st Annual IFEA Convention & Expo last week.
The International Festivals & Events Association (IFEA) announced and recognized historic Kailua Village as a 2026 IFEA World Festival & Event City during the 71st Annual IFEA Convention & Expo last week.
The prestigious IFEA World Festival & Event City Award was created to encourage, support, and recognize positive local environments for festivals and events worldwide. Festivals and events generate tremendous cultural, social, and economic value for the communities they serve, but their long-term success depends on strong partnerships and support at every level.
Nestled along the storied Kona Coast of Hawaiʻi Island, historic Kailua Village was once the seat of Hawaiian royalty and home to iconic landmarks such as Huliheʻe Palace and Mokuaikaua Church. It now serves as a dynamic gathering place for residents and visitors alike.
Whether its internationally recognized events such as the Ironman World Championship and Kona Coffee Cultural Festival or beloved community traditions, including Independence Day and Christmas parades, Kailua Village embraces the power of festivals and events to connect people.
Kailua Village demonstrates authentic Hawaiian spirit and commitment to community-driven celebrations, which enrich place and people.
“Through this program, we aim to strengthen the dialogue between events and cities around the globe, at a time when that connection has never been more important,” said IFEA President and CEO Steven Wood Schmader, CFEE, during the award presentations. “The high caliber of this year’s entries highlights the powerful role that festivals and events play in shaping vibrant, sustainable communities. The cities being honored in 2026 are setting strong examples we hope others will follow.”
Entries were reviewed by an international panel of industry experts, making this recognition the only global honor of its kind. Each city’s submission was evaluated on a comprehensive range of criteria, including:
The IFEA World Festival & Event City Award provides an international platform for communities to recognize the success of their ongoing efforts, encourage continued enhancement of festival and event infrastructure, policies, and processes, and showcase their communities as welcoming destinations for festivals and events.
For more information about the 2026 IFEA World Festival & Event City Award recipients, including recipient videos and award presentation photos, visit the IFEA World Festival & Event City Award website.

articles.content_orig:
New Skeleton Horsemen thunder into the Old World
Fresh legions of skeleton soldiers have raised by the will of the Tomb Kings, but they’re not alone. The armies of Khemri boasted squadrons of skilled cavalry, and now their desiccated remains saddle up for another charge across the sands.
This new multipart plastic kit contains 10 cavalry miniatures that can be built as either Skeleton Horsemen or Skeleton Horse Archers, each offering a different tactical option. The Horsemen can be armed with either a cavalry spear or sword to go with their shields, and the kit includes interchangeable heads, making it easy to customise your undead hordes.
You can run these miniatures as a single unit of 10 or two smaller units of five, and each set of five has enough parts to build a full command section including a champion, musician,* and banner bearer – whether Horsemen or Horse Archers.
As the unstoppable Khemrian legions march forwards with ranks of shielded warriors and regiments of archers filling the sky with deadly arrows, the Skeleton Horsemen and Horse Archers fill a vital skirmishing role by using their raw speed to sweep around enemy flanks before hitting them where it hurts the most. They’re especially effective at picking off war engine teams and vulnerable support units, while your heavier units fight over the centre ground.
The new Skeleton Horsemen will be riding into action soon. Grab a copy of Warhammer: The Old World – Ravening Hordes so that you have the rules you need to use the new miniatures in your games.
* And for those asking how can a skeleton blow a trumpet when they don’t have any lungs, the answer is simple – magic.

articles.title_orig: Rep. Ilhan Omar's home raided by DHS in fraud probe of immigration paperwork: Report
articles.title_zh: Rep. Ilhan Omar's home raided by DHS in fraud probe of immigration paperwork: Report
articles.content_orig:
Federal authorities on Monday morning raided the Washington, D.C., area home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, a Minnesota Democrat, as part of a criminal fraud investigation into her immigration paperwork filled out by her father, Fox News reported, citing a person familiar with the situation.
The Department of Justice later confirmed the raid when asked about it by CNBC.
Omar, who was born in Somalia and brought to the United States as a child, has been a target of criticism by President Donald Trump . She became a U.S. citizen in 2000, at the age of 17.
Homeland Security Investigations, a division of the Department of Homeland Security, conducted the raid, Fox News reported.
The Department of Justice, in a statement to CNBC when asked about the raid, said, "Today in the Washington, D.C., area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice."
"This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation," the statement said.
The raid comes less than a month before November's midterm elections. Omar, 44, is seeking another term as a representative for Minnesota's Fifth District.
CNBC has requested from Omar's office and the DOJ.
This is developing news. Check back for updates.

articles.title_orig: Zverev clinches ATP Year-End No. 1 presented by PIF honours
articles.title_zh: Zverev clinches ATP Year-End No. 1 presented by PIF honours
articles.content_orig:
Alexander Zverev clinched ATP Year-End No. 1 presented by PIF honours for the first time on Monday.
Eight times previously, Zverev finished inside the Top 10 of the year-end PIF ATP Rankings. On five occasions, he was inside the Top 5. Now, at the end of 2026, the 29-year-old will finish the season as World No. 1.
“It’s been a fantastic season for me winning in Paris and New York and knowing that I will finish the year on top of the rankings is just a dream come true," Zverev said. "So much work and effort have been put into achieving this goal, especially after coming back from the ankle injury. I look forward to finishing the season in style.”
Zverev became the first German to earn ATP Year-End No. 1 presented by PIF honours and the oldest player to accomplish the feat for the first time. Set to be 29 years, 217 days old on the date of the year-end PIF ATP Rankings (23 November 2026), he will be three days older than Andre Agassi was in 1999 (29 years, 214 days) and 20 days older than Andy Murray was in 2016 (29 years, 197 days).
It has been the best season of Zverev’s career, claiming his two biggest titles. The German began 2026 without a major title to his name, but he triumphed at both Roland Garros and the US Open to position himself for year-end No. 1 honours.
Zverev reached the Australian Open semi-finals in January, ultimately falling short to eventual champion Carlos Alcaraz in a five-hour, 27-minute thriller. The righty then reached at least the semi-finals at the first four ATP Masters 1000 events of the season in Indian Wells, Miami, Monte-Carlo and Madrid (where he was a finalist), losing to eventual champion Jannik Sinner on each occasion.
The Hamburg-born Zverev faced first-time major finalist Flavio Cobolli in the Roland Garros final, lifting his first Slam trophy in five sets to join Agassi, Goran Ivanisevic and Dominic Thiem in capturing his first major crown in his fourth final. He became the first man from his country to triumph at Roland Garros in the Open Era. Shortly thereafter, he made the Wimbledon final to become the first German man in history to reach the final at all four Grand Slam tournaments.
The 29-year-old needed five sets in his first two matches of the US Open , but that did not stop him from making history. Zverev dropped just one set the rest of the tournament to emerge victorious in New York, becoming only the fourth man in the Open Era to win his second major title in the same year as his first, joining Jimmy Connors (1974), Guillermo Vilas (1977) and Sinner (2024). He tallied a 25-2 record at the majors this season.
Zverev is the fourth active player to earn ATP Year-End No. 1 presented by PIF honours. Record-holder Novak Djokovic (8x), Alcaraz (2x) and Sinner (1x) have also done it.
In 2024, Zverev finished as year-end No. 2 for the first time. Two years later, he will complete the season as World No. 1.
ATP Chairman Andrea Gaudenzi said: “Finishing the season as year-end No. 1 is the ultimate achievement in our sport. Congratulations to Sascha, who became just the 20th player to do so. For a decade, he has consistently been one of the best players in the world. To finish as year-end No. 1 for the first time aged 29 shows his grit and determination to continue pushing forward.”
Later this year, Zverev will become the 30th player to reach World No. 1 in the PIF ATP Rankings, with the earliest he can achieve the feat being 2 November.
Zverev will now turn his attention to the end of the season, with plenty still at stake. The German is in the Round of 16 at the Rolex Shanghai Masters , where he is attempting to claim his eighth Masters 1000 title. At the end of 2026, he will try to become the eighth player to earn at least three Nitto ATP Finals titles.

articles.title_orig: Diné paddler honors his roots on the world stage
articles.title_zh: Diné paddler honors his roots on the world stage
articles.content_orig:
From Gallup to Singapore, Adam Becenti has found cultural connection, spiritual strength and community through competitive paddling
From Gallup to Singapore, Adam Becenti has found cultural connection, spiritual strength and community through competitive paddling
Adam Becenti, a Diné paddler from Gallup, is celebrating Indigenous Peoples Day by honoring his roots and showcasing his abilities on the global stage.
Becenti grew up playing sports commonly offered in the New Mexico desert while also participating in Diné ceremonies and learning about his culture from his father.
After moving to Portland, Oregon, in 2013, he joined a Native dragon boat team made up of Columbia River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission employees. He began outrigger canoeing in 2017, eventually finding that paddling offered more than exercise and competition.
For Becenti, the sport provides mental, physical, emotional and spiritual benefits while connecting him with Indigenous paddling traditions around the world.
"As a Diné person, we hold water sacred," Becenti said. "Every time I get on the water, I try to make an offering and ultimately connect in those ways."
Paddling has taken Becenti to Japan and New Zealand, where he has learned from other cultures and built relationships with Indigenous communities. He said those experiences showed him that paddling is more than a sport; it is a culture, lifestyle and generational tradition for many Indigenous peoples.
In August, Becenti represented the United States and the Pacific Northwest at the 2026 World Sprints. His team reached the semifinals in its strongest races.
Although the team did not advance as far as it had hoped, Becenti said competing alongside some of the world’s top paddlers and participating in cultural exchanges felt like a victory.
Now living in Seattle, Becenti paddles on Lake Washington and plans to train for distance championships and attempt to qualify for future sprint championships.
His advice to others is to travel, embrace new experiences and build relationships with people from different cultures without forgetting who they are or where they come from.

articles.title_orig: Hall, Woodford win Nobel prize for work on how to stabilise economies
articles.title_zh: Hall, Woodford win Nobel prize for work on how to stabilise economies
articles.content_orig:
American professors Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford have won the 2026 Nobel prize in economics for developing new economic models that help governments and central banks stabilize their economies to minimize the impact of external shocks.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the prize in Stockholm on Monday.
“The laureates have helped us smooth out the economy’s peaks and troughs,” the academy said in a statement , adding that their models have been “extremely helpful in dealing with the economic downturns that have affected us.”
Hall, born in Palo Alto, California in 1943, is a professor at Stanford University. Woodford, born in Chicopee, Massachusetts in 1955, is a professor at Columbia University. They will each receive 6 million Swedish kronor ($598,000) in prize money.
Their work “has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world,” noted John Hassler, the chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences.
“With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” he added.
Navi Pillay reacts to winning the Nobel Peace Prize
Rather than analyzing links between so-called “macroeconomic” variables such as inflation, production and consumption, Hall and Woodford looked to “microeconomics” to understand how the decisions of individuals and households can affect the economy.
Central to their models was the insight that households and businesses are “forward-looking” when making decisions about savings or how to price products.
Governments and central banks can influence this view of the future when communicating their plans for fiscal and monetary policy respectively and so “move the economy in the right direction,” the academy said.
The prize, officially known as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences, was not instituted by Alfred Nobel. It was established by Sweden’s central bank in 1968 and is awarded in memory of Nobel.
The number of individuals who have been awarded the prize now totals 101, only three of whom have been women. Fewer than half of the prizes awarded since 1969 have gone to one laureate only.
The economics prize concludes this year’s Nobel awards. South African judge and human rights pioneer Navi Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday. A day prior, Canadian writer Anne Carson won the Nobel Prize in literature.

articles.title_orig: Russia-Ukraine live: Zelensky says Russia hit Ukrainian power plant after Trump declared energy ceasefire
articles.title_zh: Russia-Ukraine live: Zelensky says Russia hit Ukrainian power plant after Trump declared energy ceasefire
articles.content_orig:
President Volodymyr Zelensky says Ukraine is willing to back an energy ceasefire if Moscow does the same, adding it could "become a major step toward ending the war"
However, he says Russia hit a power plant in Ukraine "immediately after" Donald Trump announced on Sunday what he called an energy ceasefire
Russia's foreign minister has said Kyiv doesn't deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring
Earlier, when asked about an energy truce, a Kremlin spokesman said : "As soon as we have something to say on the matter, we will inform you"
Our Russia editor Steve Rosenberg outlines who's saying what
Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure so Moscow can fulfil a recently struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market
Russia has ramped up attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure every winter since Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion in 2022
Edited by Kieran Kelly and Charlotte Hadfield
Joe Inwood World news correspondent
It was just over three weeks ago that President Trump signed into law the "Russia and Iran Sanctions Act".
It was named after the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham - a staunch supporter of Ukraine.
President Trump had given the eulogy at his funeral. 

The act gave the president sweeping powers to impose sanctions on any countries who bought Russian oil and gas.
Days after signing it, he told the United Nations: "If necessary, I will have to use them. It's time to stop the killing."
That is why Fridayâs announcement that President Trump had done a deal with Vladimir Putin to buy Russian diesel has been met with such fury - and accusations of betrayal and hypocrisy.

Stopping oil and gas being exported by Russia was started US policy to that point.
With a single social media post, he not only abandoned that, but promised to do the very thing the bill was trying to prevent.
The powerful Senate Foreign Relations Committee put out a statement criticising the move.

It was signed by Republican Senators and said: "The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course."
But - rather than back down, President Trump has doubled down - blaming Ukraine for the global energy crisis and calling on President Zelensky to quit.
Russia has attacked six energy facilities in Ukraine today, says President Volodymyr Zelensky.
The attacks have injured 33 people, he says.
He gives the update on social media, as part of a message thanking the European Union for adopting a new package of sanctions against Russia.
"More pressure on Russian entities" is "the right and indispensable signal if we are serious about ending Russia's war", Zelensky adds.
The EU member states have adopted nearly 1,600 new sanctions targeting Russia's military-industrial complex.
The sanctions were described by President of the European Council AntÃ³nio Costa as the "largest single-expansion" of measures against Russia since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
A firefighter at the scene of a strike on Kharkiv
Prime Minister of Ukraine Serhii Koretskyi has given an update against Russian strikes on the country both overnight and on Monday morning.
In the city of Izyum, in the Kharkiv region, one person was injured and seven houses damaged in an attack, he says.
Residential areas in the cities of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk - which sit in the Donetsk region of Donbas - were also hit, he says.
Koretskyi says a Russian drone attack on the city of Kharkiv hit a nine-storey building, with the current number of injured standing at 22 people, including two children.
Oil and gas facilities were also Russian targets across several regions - as were warehouses, logistics companies, shopping centres, railway infrastructure, gas stations and farms, he says.
Three people have been killed in a Russian strike on the Donetsk oblast, says the regional administration.
Among the dead is a 13-year-old girl, says Vadym Filashkin, who heads up the regional government, in an update on Telegram.
Four people were injured in the attack, he adds.
He says that Russia shelled the village of Cherkaske with rockets equipped with cluster munitions, one of which hit a residential home.
Ukrainian Minister of Foreign Affairs Andrii Sybiha
Ukraine's Minister of Foreign Affairs Andrii Sybiha has responded to his Russian counterpart's comments that Ukraine doesn't deserve the "respite" that a ceasefire would bring.
"[Russian Foreign Minister Sergei] Lavrov, however, has already earned a front-row seat at the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression," says Sybiha.
"The more irrelevant and cynical comments - the more evidence for the Tribunal," he adds.
Gabriela Pomeroy Live reporter
The power is out in parts of Kyiv today as Russiaâs attacks
on energy infrastructure have continued in recent weeks.
Tetiana Fisenko says she is using portable generators and camping LED lights with batteries as there is no power in her home in the city's Nyvky district.
"Last week the energy station in our district was attacked. Just near our house. It was really scary," she says.
"When Russia attacks the electricity services, we also have problems with the water."
On Sunday there was no water in her home from 1400 till 2300 local time.
"The city pump stations donât have electricity, and it's hard without water especially with a young child at home," she says, adding that the water was on and off all last week too.
On Friday, her home had no electricity for 23 hours.
"We got used to the power outages," she says, "and I really donât believe anything can stop the attacks of Russia."
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov says Russia would be willing to suspend strikes on Ukraine "specifically on election day"
Russia would only suspend strikes against Ukraine "specifically on election day", according to Vladimir Putin's spokesperson Dmitry Peskov.
"If they really want to hold elections in Kyiv, [Putin] will be ready to give an order not to carry out strikes on Ukraine on election day," Peskov said, according to Russian state news agency Tass.
"Specifically on election day. This is a very important clarification," he says, adding that 60-day ceasefire proposed by Volodymyr Zelensky would allow Ukraine to âheal its woundsâ and continue the war.
Liza Fokht BBC News Russian, Senior Reporter
Russiaâs evasive comments on the "energy ceasefire" show just how justified Ukrainian concerns were that the US had struck a diesel deal with Russia without getting anything in return.
It is already clear that the agreement to sell diesel to the US is, first and foremost, a symbolic victory for Vladimir Putin.
The Russian president can now claim that he personally helped President Trump at an important moment, while also gaining another opportunity to deepen tensions between Kyiv and Washington.
Russia also has more to gain than the potential revenue from diesel sales. More broadly, Moscowâs war effort is constrained by US intelligence-sharing with Ukraine and by the continued flow of American weapons, even if Europe is now paying for them.
But even if Moscowâs most ambitious hopes do not
materialise, the minimum objective has already been achieved: Russia is once
again striking deals with the US without any Ukrainian or European involvement,
receiving carrots rather than sticks â and without agreeing to any compromises
on ending the war.
Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov says Ukraine doesn't deserve the "respite" that a ceasefire would bring.
It comes after President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sunday that a 60-day ceasefire would allow â his âcountry to hold presidential elections, following comments from President Donald Trump that "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president" .
Zelensky said that from a security standpoint, holding elections is "completely impossible" as there are attacks "day and night", as he called for a "full ceasefire

articles.title_orig: Mato’s AI Talent Interviews Humans
articles.title_zh: Mato’s AI Talent Interviews Humans
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › News and Business › News Makers
Mato is a media platform that uses AI to help companies turn their expertise into professionally produced podcasts and media.
“We’re building the first generation of AI talents that interview real humans, creating authentic content at a scale that was never before possible,” it states.
Mato has been awarded an ElevenLabs grant, received AWS Activate credits and is a member of NVIDIA Inception.
Alexander Benz is co-founder and CEO.
Radio World: What is Mato?
Alexander Benz: Mato is a Los Angeles-based media technology company founded in 2024 by my husband, Edward Benz, and me. The company is privately held, and we recently raised a pre-seed investment from Mucker Capital and joined MuckerLab .
Mato gives companies AI agents that interview real human guests live. The AI host prepares for the subject, conducts an unscripted interview, listens to what the guest actually says, and asks followup questions in real time. The conversation can then move through editing, transcripts, clips, cover art and distribution, with the customer retaining final approval.
RW: Tell us more about it and how it might be used by radio broadcasters or related audio fields.
Benz: The core product is the live AI interviewer.
Most AI audio tools start with text and generate something from it. Mato starts with a person. A real guest joins an interview, speaks naturally, and the AI host conducts the conversation in real time.
A public demonstration of the AI interviewer is available , which includes a Kevin DeMeritt interview, transcript and follow-up timestamps.
For radio, I think the interesting part is what that does to the economics and logistics of producing expert-led audio. A broadcaster can capture interviews, recurring expert segments, branded programming or niche shows without needing a human host and full production team around every recording session.
Since we first spoke, we’ve brought this into traditional radio with Lear Capital. Their Mato-produced show “ Outside the Dollar ” uses AI-hosted interviews with real guests and is now being distributed for radio as well as digital listening.
RW: What prompted the development of a tool that uses an AI host to conduct interviews?
Benz: We were much more interested in whether AI could conduct a good conversation than whether it could generate another piece of content.
There is an enormous amount of useful knowledge sitting inside companies with founders, customers, executives and subject-matter experts. Traditional podcast production makes capturing that knowledge relatively expensive and operationally heavy.
The question became: What happens if the AI does the preparation, interviewing and much of the production work, while the expertise still comes from an actual person?
RW: How do your guardrails assure that the final interview is correct and appropriate?
Benz: We do not claim that an AI interviewer can guarantee that every statement a guest makes is factually correct.
Our approach is to preserve provenance and human editorial control instead.
The recorded human conversation remains the source. Customers can set the subject, questions and editorial boundaries before an interview, and they retain final approval before anything is released. The transcript and recording also make it possible to review the finished material against what the guest actually said.
The AI is responsible for conducting and processing the conversation. It does not become the authority on the subject being discussed.
RW: What is the experience of being interviewed by an AI host like?
Benz: It feels much closer to being interviewed by a person than completing a questionnaire or talking to a traditional chatbot.
The guest joins, the AI host asks a question, and the guest answers naturally. While they are speaking, the agent is listening to the substance of the answer and deciding what makes sense to ask next.
So if someone introduces an unexpected detail, the host can follow that thread rather than simply moving to question number three on a predetermined list.
The guest does not need to write prompts or learn how to use an AI tool. Their job is simply to talk about what they know.
RW: How can an interested reader learn more or hear an example?
Benz: Lear Capital’s “Outside the Dollar” is a useful current example because it shows the model in an actual subject-matter interview rather than a scripted demonstration.
We also have several public interviews and product examples available through Mato, along with a press kit containing screenshots and company information.
RW: What else should we know?
Benz: The distinction that matters most to us is that we are not trying to synthesize the human out of media.
There are already plenty of AI products that can generate an article, a voice or a podcast from a prompt. Mato is built around the opposite premise: The interesting material should still come from a real person.
We want AI to remove much of the coordination and production work required to capture that person’s knowledge, rather than replacing the person whose knowledge made the content worth producing in the first place.
Podcasting is our first use case, but we see the broader product as a conversation layer for capturing human knowledge.

articles.title_orig: Why Real-World Evidence Matters for Nonhormonal Menopause VMS Therapy
articles.title_zh: Why Real-World Evidence Matters for Nonhormonal Menopause VMS Therapy
articles.content_orig:
Pauline M. Maki, PhD, introduces OPTION-VMS and explains why real-world data are needed to test whether randomized trial findings for nonhormonal VMS therapy generalize to everyday patients.
Welcome back to another Contemporary OB/GYN Investigator Perspectives series. In this opening segment, Pauline M. Maki, PhD, professor of psychiatry, psychology, and obstetrics and gynecology at the University of Illinois Chicago, where she directs the Center for Health Awareness and Research on Menopause, discusses real-world evidence for nonhormonal treatment of vasomotor symptoms (VMS) of menopause.
Maki introduces OPTION-VMS, which she describes as the first real-world evidence to include fezolinetant (Veozah) among nonhormonal menopausal therapies. She outlines what the study reveals about VMS bother, mood, and sleep; how its preliminary data and updated data cuts connect; why objective actigraphy adds a dimension to sleep assessment beyond patient-reported outcomes; and what the findings mean for counseling patients in everyday ob-gyn practice.
She begins by explaining why the study was needed. The randomized, placebo-controlled trial remains the gold standard for understanding the effects of a new medication, Maki notes, because the placebo arm shows what improvement can be expected by chance for outcomes such as hot flashes, mood, and sleep. That design establishes whether a medication works, the magnitude of improvement, and the health indications it improves. The SKYLIGHT trials took this approach and showed the efficacy of fezolinetant on VMS and sleep.
The next question, Maki explains, is how those results translate to the women practitioners treat in their clinics. Clinical trials must select relatively healthy participants, who may differ from the typical patients clinicians see, and many groups of women do not participate in clinical trials for a variety of reasons. This raises the question of external generalizability: whether findings observed in a clinical trial hold for the types of women who walk through a clinic door. That, she says, is what OPTION-VMS was designed to test.
In the next segment, Maki reviews what the first OPTION-VMS data cuts show about hot flash bother, work productivity, depression, and anxiety.
