articles.title_orig: The man hiking the world in search of rare cheeses
articles.title_zh: The man hiking the world in search of rare cheeses
articles.content_orig:
Trevor Warmedahl has spent years documenting rare and traditional cheesemaking methods, and believes that "cheese is an edible manifestation of a place".
Trevor Warmedahl was working as a commercial cheesemaker in Seattle when he realised he was using milk that came from animals he never saw. So, he quit his job and set off on what has become a global odyssey to discover places that still make cheese the old-fashioned way.
In 2019 he arrived in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, and lived alone in a yurt with a dog as his companion. He soon discovered that dairy was sacred there: the women flicked milk into the air before cheesemaking, a gesture of respect called a milk libation . He visited homes where whey bubbled over central hearths and fresh, unripened byaslag cheese covered tables. After hiking to shrines, he noticed people offered dairy products as a symbol of purity.
As summer unfolded and city-dwellers migrated to the Mongolian steppe to farm, Warmedahl itched to join. He jumped on a Soviet-era coal-powered sleeper train for a rickety overnight ride across the Gobi Desert. On the journey back to Ulaanbaatar, he met a local who invited him to stay with her herder family on the Zavkhan grassland.
Warmedahl spent that summer waking before dawn to milk yaks, chasing livestock up the valley on horses, listening to shepherds' folk songs at sunset and cooking milk into dehydrated, sweet-and-sour curds called aaruul . The experience inspired him to seek out other places preserving rare cheesemaking traditions before they disappeared.
During the past six years, Warmedahl has hitched, hiked and driven through more than 20 countries, documenting traditional cheesemaking and pastoral lifestyles, and offering workshops on natural dairy processing . After recently completing a 193km (120-mile) cheese trek across the Peaks of the Balkans Trail , he shared with the BBC what cheesemaking reveals about a place.
You've been to so many places – Bulgaria, Pakistan, Italy, Austria, Cambodia. Share a standout adventure.
Ancestral cheeses in Georgia have no analogues – I call them "fossil cheeses" because they were almost lost but are making a comeback as part of a broader post-Soviet cultural revival. My pinnacle moment happened in Tusheti, a mountain region bordering Russia near the tourist village of Omalo.
I showed up with vague directions to the shepherds' summer camp, which was deep in the valley. That's a theme: the cheeses I find are always far out, made by hermit types sticking to the old ways out of sheer stubbornness. It was drop-dead gorgeous, just me and my backpack. The valley ends on an abrupt cliff, with deteriorating medieval stone towers. Shepherds build their camps from the decay. I saw how these guys milked sheep by hand with wooden pails, rustic-style. It's a feta-like cheese called Tushuri guda , aged in inside-out sheepskins. At the end of the season, I walked about 130km (81 miles) back down the valley with them and 300 sheep. The herd has done this for generations – they know where to go. The shepherds just coordinated, and it created this crazy lawless feeling with dogs barking and me, chasing stray sheep down ravines.
At night we'd build a campfire and drink, and even with the language barrier, we'd relate through food. Sometimes language isn't needed. In cheesemaking, if two hearts want to connect, they'll find a way.
How is cheese and cheesemaking a reflection of a community's history and culture?
Cheese is a sensory experience and embodies larger ideas about how we live. It represents how meaningful human cultures can be. At its best, cheese reflects this complex relationship between humans, landscapes, microbial life and livestock at a time [when] we've become so separate from how food is made. And the cultural element holds the constellation together.
The cheeses I highlight represent an older mentality, with a sense of stewardship over the places we live and farm. So, a little bit more of the wildness of nature slips into the product. [Cheese is] an edible manifestation of place, of cultural history transformed into delicious food.
Why is cheesemaking especially important today?
The diversity and range of cheese is infinite. When animals eat, they transform grass and entire landscapes into milk that becomes cheese, and animals can graze [almost] anywhere. So, it's a lifestyle that can move in response to climate uncertainty and desertification – real challenges today.
The cheeses I focus on – natural farmstead cheeses [made exclusively with milk from a farmer's own animals] – reflect deep, ethical relationships between people and livestock and highlight the incredible diversity of heritage livestock. With industrialisation, that diversity is vanishing at an alarming rate. So pastoral cheesemaking strikes me as profoundly sustainable.
What can so-called "exotic cheeses" that challenge us reveal about a place?
There's this greyish-brown cheese from Norway, gammelost , [covered in] moulds like fruit rot. It tastes like a musty cellar with bold, mouth-numbing spiciness. It wasn't for me. But deliciousness is cultural. It's taught. So, I always say: don't try something once, try it 10 times. Uncomfortable foods open doors. But be sure to eat them because you're interested in the culture, not because they're freaky to you.
One of the easiest ways to express interest in a culture is to say: feed me what you eat. When people realise you're genuine, the relationship deepens and you begin to understand their history through food. Funky cheeses become cultural emblems because of how obscure and special they are.
You set out on your global cheese journey without a real plan. What did this approach add to your experience?
Back then [in 2019], I was hopping on a whim from one volunteer gig to the next, drawn to remote places where people worked to protect and revitalise traditional cheeses. Workaway on farms, or staying for a while at guesthouses where cheese is made, are still amazing ways to go beyond tourism to see how people really live.
Cheese gives you access to a global community, like at [the Slow Food Cheese Festival in] Bra, Italy. But anything you can do to find that deeper experience – food, handicrafts – is worth it, even if you can't always plan in advance. If your heart is in the right place and you jump fully into adventure when it calls, the details will almost always work themselves out.
What advice would you give fellow travellers about how to best experience unique cheeses abroad?
Find the cheese shop or cheesemonger that has the most local tilt and ask them which cheesemakers you can and should visit. Organising it yourself is cheaper. But there are also paid tours where you can experience a range of cheeses in a short period and really get to know a place. Just make sure that the cost actually supports local producers – that's what I call responsible "lacto-culinary" tourism.
How can other travellers seek out responsible agrotourism experiences?
Look for local cheesemakers and guides. It's also important to not expect farmers to sanitise things. It's normal to go to a farm and see broken-down equipment and mud. When we romanticise tradition, it encourages locals to put themselves in a museum. But tools [and] tradition have always evolved.
• The elusive cheese with no recipe
• Is cheese the new reason to travel?
• The woman saving Georgia's lost cheeses
We need to be open to the fact that it's not all grandmas spinning wool on wheels outside stone cottages. Then it becomes kind of a show, and we're pushing farmers to become something they're not for tourists.
What places have exciting, overlooked, or under-the-radar cheeses? Where are you keen to travel next?
Hands down, Turkey . It's a universe of cheese that doesn't get enough attention. Tulum peyniri is emblematic of pastoral lifestyles and the extreme sacrifice at the root of dairying and – I'd argue – life. That's because it's aged mainly in furry goatskins, so it looks insane bec

articles.title_orig: WATCH: Pope Leo XIV Marks 100 Years of World Mission Sunday
articles.title_zh: WATCH: Pope Leo XIV Marks 100 Years of World Mission Sunday
articles.content_orig:
In a new video for the centennial, Pope Leo reflects on his personal connection to World Mission Sunday, from his childhood in the United States to his years of missionary service in Peru.
Ahead of the 100th World Mission Sunday on the weekend of October 17-18, Pope Leo XIV released a personal video message reflecting on the extraordinary day.
100 years ago, when World Mission Sunday began, there were about 9.6 million Catholics living in 296 mission jurisdictions. Today, that number has grown to more than 346 million Catholics living in 1,131 mission territories.
These individuals are served through more than 41,000 parishes, 124,309 Catholic schools and 26, 318 social institutions.
When he was a child, Pope Leo XIV celebrated World Mission Sunday in the United States. Later, when he was a priest and bishop in Peru, he was the recipient of the generous prayers and support of Catholics around the world.
Now, as pope, he celebrates the centennial of the mission-supporting international collection and expresses gratitude for the Church's loving support of our brothers and sisters worldwide.
To support World Mission Sunday, Catholics across Northern Colorado may donate to their parish with "World Mission Sunday" in the memo line of their donation. For more information, visit the Pontifical Mission Societies' website here .

articles.title_orig: Invenra Launches "52 Views of Cancer" Art Deck at World ADC Conference
articles.title_zh: Invenra Launches "52 Views of Cancer" Art Deck at World ADC Conference
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Patient-inspired playing cards connect cancer experiences with drug discovery as Invenra introduces its multispecific ADC program
MADISON, Wis., October 12, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )--Invenra Inc., a biotechnology company developing multispecific antibody therapeutics, announced the launch of its first 52 Views of Cancer , a playing card deck showcasing original artwork by people affected by cancer. Invenra is debuting the deck at the World ADC Conference in San Diego.
The project links cancer journeys directly to researchers, clinicians, and drug developers. The launch also marks the company's expansion into antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) asset discovery, using its powerful B-Body® bispecific and T-Body™ trispecific antibody discovery platforms to create next-generation multispecific ADC assets for development with biopharma partners.
Art connects patients and researchers
Each of the deck's 52 cards, along with the jokers and box cover, features original artwork contributed by a different cancer patient, survivor, or family member. Together, the works celebrate the creativity, resilience, and spirit of people whose lives have been touched by cancer.
"Through this project, we want to bring the experiences of people affected by cancer into the conversations shaping new cancer therapies," said Roland Green, Invenra CEO and founder. "The deck also introduces our work in antibody-drug conjugates. Invenra is developing ADCs for a wide variety of cancers, including ovarian, breast, lung, colon, neuroblastoma, osteosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, Ewing's sarcoma, diffuse midline glioma, and glioblastoma."
Invenra licensed the artwork and offered an honorarium to each featured artist. The artwork and accompanying stories are available on the 52 Views project website.
Invenra is sharing the decks at the conference and other major scientific and medical conferences, placing patients' voices and perspectives directly in the hands of researchers, clinicians, and scientists working to cure the cancers these artists have experienced.
Advancing multispecific ADC discovery
The Invenra ADC discovery program combines its collection of antibody binders with proprietary multispecific platforms to develop candidates that enable access to broader patient populations with wider coverage by targeting multiple tumor targets.
Additionally, the company's T-Body platform supports development of trispecific constructs incorporating HYPER-Internalization™ mechanisms, which can increase internalization, delivering more payload to cells while simultaneously targeting multiple pathways to reduce tumor escape routes.
On October 13, 2026, at the World ADC Conference, Bonnie Hammer, PhD, Invenra Executive Vice President of R&D, will present new preclinical data on the company's ADC programs. In her talk, entitled From Bispecific to Trispecific Antibodies: Reimagining the Next Generation of ADCs , Hammer outlines a novel HER2 × HER2 × HER3 T-Body trispecific antibody, which combines three binders to target breast cancer.
"The preclinical data demonstrate the amazing potential of trispecific ADCs," said Hammer. "Invenra is exploring how trispecific targeting can improve payload delivery and address signaling pathways that may contribute to treatment resistance."
Invenra is a biotechnology company focused on the discovery and development of multispecific antibody therapeutics. Invenra employs its extensive technology toolbox and efficient discovery engine to design and create potential first- and best-in-class drug candidates. The Invenra T-Body platform expands these capabilities for efficient expression, correct chain pairing, and robust assembly of trispecific constructs. Invenra partners globally with pharmaceutical and biotech companies to accelerate therapeutic antibody programs from discovery through preclinical development and is developing therapeutic assets, including ADCs, for licensing. For more information, visit www.invenra.com .

articles.title_zh: AI System Could Transform Rabies Testing Around the World | Newswise
articles.content_orig:
Newswise — Rabies virus detection in cell cultures could soon become faster and more accessible, thanks to a world-first AI system developed by researchers at the University of Surrey’s Institute for People-Centred AI (PAI) in collaboration with the Rabies and Viral Zoonoses team at the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA). The breakthrough is designed to help improve surveillance of one of the world’s deadliest infectious diseases and deliver practical, laboratory-ready tools that can be adopted in endemic countries.
Despite being almost entirely preventable through vaccination, rabies causes around 59,000 human deaths every year. Current practices for diagnosis and measuring protective antibodies through vaccination still rely on specialists manually examining thousands of microscope images – which can be slow, labour-intensive and open to differences in interpretation.
In a DEFRA-funded study published in Nature Scientific Reports, the research team created the first AI-based workflow capable of identifying rabies virus infection in cell cultures and accurately measuring antibody concentration levels.
Using more than 2,300 fluorescence images containing over 36,000 annotated image sections, the team trained several deep learning models to recognise rabies virus infection within cells. The best-performing model correctly classified 99.6 per cent of samples and almost perfectly distinguished infected from uninfected cells, avoiding false alarms.
Joan Amaya-Cuesta, PhD researcher at the University of Surrey and Rabies and Viral Zoonoses Research Scientist at the APHA, said:
"Rabies is one of the world’s oldest and deadliest infectious diseases, claiming tens of thousands of lives every year because timely diagnosis and surveillance remain challenging in many parts of the world. Once clinical signs appear, it is almost always fatal, so prevention and early diagnosis are essential.
"Our AI workflow provides laboratories with a faster and more consistent way to analyse samples while reducing the reliance on manual interpretation."
The technology could help laboratories analyse samples more quickly and consistently, particularly in countries where rabies remains endemic and specialist expertise is limited. It could also reliably measure antibody levels used to assess vaccine protection and support international pet travel requirements.
Professor Miroslaw Bober, Professor of Video Processing and Machine Intelligence at the University of Surrey, said:
"This research shows how AI can support scientists by carrying out complex image analysis quickly, consistently and at scale. While we've demonstrated this approach for rabies, the same framework could be applied to other infectious diseases that rely on similar laboratory tests, helping researchers and diagnostic laboratories make better use of AI in the future."
The results establish a framework that can be adapted for the detection, analysis, and surveillance of other pathogens, supporting broader applications of AI across infectious disease research and diagnostics.
Dr Lorraine M. McElhinney, Head of the National Reference Laboratory for Human and Animal Rabies at the APHA, said:
“We hope this innovation will help strengthen rabies surveillance and, ultimately, support global efforts to eliminate human deaths from this disease. This technology is now being further developed for use to detect the virus in infected brain tissue which we hope will transform international rabies diagnostic laboratories.”

articles.title_orig: Nikon revokes first prize in Small World in Motion video competition over AI use
articles.title_zh: Nikon revokes first prize in Small World in Motion video competition over AI use
articles.content_orig:
The winner of a prestigious scientific photography competition has been disqualified after organizers concluded that his use of generative AI broke the rules.
Ning Xu was named the winner of the annual Nikon Small World in Motion competition in September, but his video received a number of critical comments from experts who questioned its use of AI.
Nikon launched an investigation, and announced its conclusion in a statement Friday.
“After thoroughly re-evaluating the video and supporting materials and consulting with members of our judging panel, Nikon has determined that the winning video did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI,” the statement reads, adding that the competition rankings have been adjusted.
“This decision is based solely on the submitted video’s eligibility under the rules outlined for this competition. It should not be interpreted as a judgment of the entrant’s professional reputation, scientific contributions, or intent,” it said.
Nikon also said it would revisit its rules and evaluation procedures for the annual competition in future.
The new winner is a video showing a tiny roundworm and a single-celled Dileptus, a kind of single-celled microorganism, by Vietnamese researcher Nguyen Nam Nhat.
Xu’s video captures the abnormal beating of airway cilia — hairlike structures that protrude from cells within the human body — in a child living with primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD), a rare genetic disorder.
When Nikon posted the video on LinkedIn, it attracted criticism from scientists such as Edward Phelps, an associate professor at the University of Florida, who said there were “many serious problems with this video.”
Winner of Nikon microscopy photo contest faces criticism over AI usage
Phelps said that some of the biological structures shown in the footage do not behave as expected. “The microscopy community deserves an explanation from Nikon,” Phelps added.
In response, in a series of comments on LinkedIn, Xu acknowledged that he had used AI.
“AI was not used to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion,” he wrote.
“It was applied afterwards to the reconstructed grayscale data to distinguish and color structures with similar morphology,” he added.
CNN has reached out to Xu, who now works at the National University of Singapore as a research fellow, for further comment.

articles.title_orig: Sea World starts building marine wildlife hospital on Gold Coast
articles.title_zh: Sea World starts building marine wildlife hospital on Gold Coast
articles.content_orig:
New facility will care for sick and injured marine wildlife
Construction is underway on a new world-class marine wildlife hospital at Sea World in Australia
Construction is underway on a new world-class marine wildlife hospital at Sea World on Australia's Gold Coast.
The new Sea World Foundation Wildlife Hospital is expected to open next year and will serve as the Southern Hemisphere's first facility of its kind.
It will provide specialist care for sick and injured marine wildlife , including dolphins, whales, dugongs, rays, turtles, seabirds and sharks.
Purpose-built for rapid rescue and rehabilitation, the new facility will feature specialist equipment to treat larger marine mammals.
Queensland’s environment minister Andrew Powell said: “Shovels are in the ground at Sea World, with work underway on a world-class marine wildlife hospital that will give more sick and injured wildlife the specialist care they need."
As well as caring for marine wildlife, the hospital will give Sea World visitors the opportunity to see marine conservation and rehabilitation for themselves.
"This is a win for wildlife and a win for Queensland, supporting wildlife rehabilitation while creating new education opportunities and showcasing our conservation efforts to millions of visitors each year," Powell added.
Sea World is owned by Australia-based theme park operator Village Roadshow Group.
The new Sea World Foundation Wildlife Hospital is expected to open next year on the Gold Coast Sea World Foundation
Village Roadshow Group 's CEO Clark Kirby said: "For more than 30 years, Sea World has been at the forefront of marine rescue and rehabilitation efforts around Australia, and this project will allow our team to have an even greater impact on Australian marine life.
“The state-of-the-art facility will allow our specialised veterinary and marine animal experts to help more animals and educate the millions of guests who visit Sea World on conservation efforts to minimise impacts on the environment."
He added: “We have already rescued hundreds of marine animals this year, ranging from whales, dolphins, dugongs, turtles, seabirds and sea snakes, and with marine wildlife being under more threat than before, this new facility will greatly expand our capabilities.”

articles.title_orig: Fire Devastates the Oldest Covered Food Market in Paris
articles.title_zh: Fire Devastates the Oldest Covered Food Market in Paris
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
A massive fire has destroyed Marché des Enfants Rouges in Paris , the capital’s oldest covered food market.
Emergency services were called to the scene in the city's 3rd arrondissement at approximately 4.15am on Monday and arrived to find the market totally ablaze, local media reported.
More than 150 firefighters and 50 emergency vehicles were deployed to tackle the fire, which consumed approximately 1,000 square metres of space and caused at least two-thirds of the market's metal structure to collapse.
Paris Centre mayor Ariel Weil confirmed on X that while the fire was brought under control by morning, the market had been “ravaged” and was “totally destroyed.”
"The covered market has been completely destroyed. There is nothing left," Lieutenant-Colonel Pierre de Bouvier told French news outlet BFMTV , noting that flames were already scorching “the entire covered market” when firefighting crews reached the scene.
Fire crews worked through the morning to prevent the inferno from spreading to adjoining residential buildings along Rue de Bretagne.
No civilian casualties were reported, though one firefighter received medical attention at the scene after feeling unwell, according to emergency services.
Founded in 1615 under King Louis XIII, the site derived its name — "Market of the Red Children" — from a nearby 16th-century orphanage where children wore red uniforms.
Listed as an official historic monument in 1982, the covered market in the Haut-Marais district housed fresh produce stalls, florists, and international food stalls.
Authorities have urged the public to avoid the surrounding area while emergency crews pick through the wreckage to ensure no further risk of fire.
French authorities have opened an official investigation to establish the cause of the fire, which currently remains unknown.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | Quantum-Computing Company IonQ to Buy Cybersecurity Firm for Up to $1.3 Billion
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Quantum-Computing Company IonQ to Buy Cybersecurity Firm for Up to $1.3 Billion
articles.content_orig:
College Park, Md. - Oct. 12, 2026 - IonQ (NYSE: IONQ), the world’s leading full-stack quantum platform and foundry, today announced that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Elisity, Inc., a Zero Trust security company, in an all-stock transaction valued at up to $1.3 billion. The acquisition brings together IonQ's post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD) capabilities with Elisity's enterprise Zero Trust technology platform. On a combined basis, IonQ will benefit from an expanded cybersecurity platform that both uncovers and protects against present LLM and emerging quantum threats.
Elisity builds on IonQ’s expanding quantum security offerings with a high-growth enterprise security business, cutting-edge Zero Trust technology platform, and team of industry leaders led by cybersecurity expert CEO James Winebrenner. Elisity has a strong track record of doubling its revenue and its customer base year-over-year with zero churn among deployed customers. With more than 100 global customer deployments and deep CISO and security community relationships, Elisity will provide IonQ with expanded channels to bring its PQC, QKD and quantum computing offerings to market for both enterprise and government networks, opening up the more than $10 billion microsegmentation opportunity with double-digit CAGR to IonQ.
“With Elisity and its team as part of IonQ, we will be well positioned to help customers protect critical infrastructure and enterprise networks throughout the transition to the quantum era. As I said first, Q-Day is coming much faster than predicted. IonQ is offering its customers a vertically integrated full-stack quantum platform across quantum computing, networking, sensing and cybersecurity. Just as adding SkyWater Technology expanded IonQ’s capabilities in chip design, fabrication and packaging, Elisity will bring proven enterprise policy enforcement scale and deployment experience to our quantum security strategy and will give IonQ a strong growth platform to serve customers and create value for our shareholders,” said Niccolo de Masi, Chairman and CEO of IonQ.
“Our customers need to prioritize post-quantum cryptography initiatives while securing existing assets to keep essential operations running,” said James Winebrenner, CEO of Elisity. “With IonQ, we will be optimally positioned to partner with them to modernize their crypto-agility programs, accelerate post-quantum cryptography capabilities while advancing their holistic Zero Trust posture and deploy hybrid-cybersecurity solutions today that are prepared for the quantum future.”
Elisity’s Commercial Advantage
Enterprises face two overlapping priorities: containing attacks that operate at machine speed and preparing to protect sensitive information against future quantum threats. The urgency of this transition is underscored by recent White House executive orders advancing quantum innovation and accelerating the federal government's migration to PQC. These directives reinforce the importance of securing critical systems and preparing government networks for quantum-era threats while supporting long-term modernization.
Today, Elisity IdentityGraph combines native asset identity and partner-enriched context, and risk information to inform least-privilege access policy for users, devices, workloads and AI agents. Teams can simulate policies before limiting each identity to the communications it needs, helping reduce attack surface and contain an attack’s spread. By bringing together Elisity's Zero Trust framework with IonQ's PQC and QKD capabilities, the companies will combine cryptographic protection for sensitive information and communications with identity-based controls that limit unauthorized access and the spread of threats across enterprise networks. The shared roadmap with IonQ will extend IdentityGraph with cryptographic inventory and risk information. This integrated approach will help customers address quantum-related security risks through a multiyear transition while strengthening defenses against current cyberattacks, including threats involving AI agents.
Following closing, Elisity will continue serving its customers under its current leadership, including current CEO James Winebrenner. Together, the companies will continue their track record of innovation, customer success and strong partner relationships, backed by IonQ’s demonstrated approach of investing in the critical technologies it acquires.
IonQ’s Multiproduct Revenue Growth Opportunity
IonQ brings an established track record in growing its quantum security and quantum-secure communications offering. The company has deployed some of the largest quantum-safe national communications networks in the world, including in Switzerland, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, and serves global customers with quantum-safe defense in depth spanning quantum-safe posture management, quantum key distribution, and post quantum cryptography.
Customers are increasingly adopting multiple IonQ products and services, driving growth in multiproduct revenue and providing evidence of demand for integrated solutions; in the second quarter of 2026, IonQ delivered 40% year-over-year growth in multiproduct revenue..
IonQ and Elisity expect opportunities to cross-sell complementary security solutions, expand relationships with enterprise and government customers, and develop integrated offerings.
Under the terms of the agreement, IonQ will acquire Elisity in an all-stock transaction valued at up to $1.3 billion, including up to $150 million in earnout opportunity subject to performance of the Elisity business. The number of IonQ shares to be issued in the transaction will be calculated at closing based on the volume weighted average price of IonQ common stock for the 20 trading days prior to, but not including, the third business day before the closing date, but that price will not be greater than $49.61 or less than $33.07 per share.
The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026 and is subject to customary closing conditions, including receipt of required regulatory approval.
Elisity helps enterprises advance Zero Trust security for users, devices, workloads, AI agents and other non-human identities. Elisity IdentityGraph correlates identity, asset and risk information from native and partner sources to inform access decisions. Elisity’s software policy layer uses the network to enforce access rules independently of the underlying network technology. Teams can simulate policies and limit each identity to the communications it needs, extending the value of existing network and security investments. Founded in 2019, Elisity has a global employee footprint and a growing number of customers in the Fortune 500. Learn more at elisity.com .
IonQ, Inc . [NYSE: IONQ] is the world’s leading quantum platform and foundry - delivering integrated quantum solutions across computing, networking, sensing, and security. IonQ’s newest generation of quantum computers, the Superion, is the latest in a line of cutting-edge systems. Earlier systems have helped customers and partners including Amazon Web Services, AstraZeneca, and NVIDIA achieve a 20x performance increase over previous quantum solutions and accelerate innovation in drug discovery, materials science, financial modeling, logistics, cybersecurity, and defense. In 2025, the company achieved 99.99% two-qubit gate fidelity, setting a world record in quantum computing performance .
Headquartered in College Park, Maryland, IonQ has operations across North America, Latin America, EMEA, and APAC. Our quantum computing services have been available through all major cloud providers since 2021, while we also meet the needs of networking and sensing customers across land, sea, air, and space. IonQ is making quantum platforms more accessible and impactful than ever before. Learn more at IonQ.com .

articles.title_orig: Love blooms on a hostile colony world in As You Wake, Break the Shell
articles.title_zh: Love blooms on a hostile colony world in As You Wake, Break the Shell
articles.content_orig:
Love blooms on a hostile colony world in As You Wake, Break the Shell
Sci-fi author Becky Chambers on designing believable ecosystems, balancing scientific accuracy with emotional impact and emphasizing empathy over spectacle
By Sam Macdonald edited by Sarah Lewin Frasier
One of science fiction’s oldest themes is its insistence that the future isn’t inevitable. Few contemporary authors embody that idea more than Becky Chambers , whose stories imagine alternative futures—not through grand revolutions or galaxy-spanning battles but through ordinary people trying to care for one another.
As a defining voice of the “hopepunk” genre, Chambers has built a reputation for science fiction that prizes empathy as much as imagination. Her latest novel, As You Wake, Break the Shell , brings us to the hostile, unpredictable world of Fortune, where acid rain falls and billowing volcanoes shroud the horizon. The story follows a reclusive botanist and a spacefaring pilot across alternating timelines as they search for connection and purpose, attempting to navigate a life where Fortune has never favored the bold.
We caught up with Chambers to discuss a toxic planet’s world-building, scientific accuracy in storytelling and the motivational merits of unrelenting spite.
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing . By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
[ An edited transcript of the interview follows .]
This story spends a lot of time on a colony planet with a poisonous atmosphere. What does designing an ecosystem teach you about designing a civilization?
Everything. It’s really important for me to start with what the environmental conditions are because that’s going to affect everything from what we’re eating, what we’re building houses out of, what kind of clothes we have—and all of those things, in turn, affect culture. There is so much about our values, our personalities, that are actually molded by the physical environments we exist in, both natural and constructed.
Starting from [the questions] “what do we have” and “what do we not have” is really important for me. Suppose someone’s eating a sandwich. What’s in the sandwich? It’s a throwaway line that seems like it doesn’t matter, but it’s actually really important to say whether or not there’s lettuce in this sandwich, because that does communicate a lot of information about how this world works.
For this book, I had a really big table of crops [to reference], what are we growing, how are we growing it, what’s available and what’s not?
Those are details I spend a lot of time sussing out before I really get into the thick of drafting the story.
What specific ideas inspired the scientific foundation for this story?
Botany is the big one. I have always had an appreciation for plants but not any actual sort of technical knowledge about what it is that I’m looking at. So I did a lot of research for this book into how plants work, and specifically into seeds, which is a topic I have become fascinated by the more I learn about it. Seeds are a big part of this book, as are plants and the way they communicate with each other.
How does scientific accuracy influence your storytelling? Do you often find yourself molding the plot to fit the science, or vice versa?
I look at science as partially a foundation but more of a tool that I use to color the world that I’m in. I want it to feel tangible and possible, but I’m very willing to take some liberties here and there for the sake of getting the feeling across.
I tend to think of what I’m doing as more like impressionism than photorealism. If you think of something like Monet’s Water Lilies, for example, it doesn’t look like a real pond, right? But it feels like a real pond. And I often use a similar approach with my work. I am not necessarily painting you a picture of the cosmos as it actually exists, but what I’m trying to communicate is the sense of wonder and awe that I feel when I’m experiencing those things in the real world. So it’s a matter of getting the emotional quality of discovery across, and sometimes that does mean taking shortcuts.
With As You Wake Break the Shell , I kept it within the realm of “with sufficient technology, this could be possible.” Is it probable? Probably not. There are a lot of things that I gloss over because they’re not things that everyday people outside of science would know about or understand. We know [in the reality of the story] that there are giant space-dwelling creatures out there. We don’t need to know how it is that they evolved or what kind of world it is that they came from. Those are questions that interest me as a person who is into real science, but they don’t serve the story.
This book has a knack for taking the unknown and making it feel familiar while making the familiar feel unknown, simply by showing it from a new perspective—for instance, that of an enormous, cargo-toting space behemoth. How do you get into the headspace of examining humanity from the outside?
It’s a highly technical process that involves me sitting in my armchair and just staring at the ceiling and thinking about what it would be like to have a body other than mine, and just sort of deconstructing everything that makes me down to the raw components and trying to figure out what it is that’s necessary and what’s not.
I take a lot of inspiration from the natural world. I have a really keen interest in invertebrate life and in deep-sea life, and I have a real interest in animal intelligence that exists in nonmammalian creatures.
What would it mean to communicate through color? What would it mean to communicate through pheromones? What does the world feel like if you don’t have a sense of sight like we do? I just love taking any one of those traits and then expanding it to make something that we would recognize as a person, regardless of whether they physically look like us or not. How does that make you think about yourself? How does that make you think about existence?
As You Wake, Break the Shell is a love story as much as a space story. What did pairing those genres let you explore that you couldn’t do with either one on their own?
It allowed me the freedom to not segment any of the things I was thinking of into separate boxes. This was a really personal book for me in that I’m writing about everything I care about in this one. I’m writing about the natural world, I’m writing about society, and I am also writing about love, romantic love, and these are all things that are extremely important to me in my everyday life.
We have a bazillion stories about “and then they lived happily ever after,” but I actually want to see what that looks like because it’s never that simple.I feel that the most interesting parts of a relationship are what happens “after,” and so that was what drove a large part of my decision to have [the book] be a split timeline, where it’s very clear from the jump that they’re going to be together a long time and we’re going to see all these different stages in what makes them them, because I do think that that’s an area that is underexplored.
You’ve said before that you write the stories that you need to hear. What did you need to hear from this book?
I wanted to see a relationship that matched my own. Queer representation in media is better than ever in a lot of ways, and yet it’s still very rare to see anybody over their 20s.
By the time we started getting more stories about coming of age or people falling in love when they’re young, I was already too old for those stories. I was feeling a real frustration in not finding love stories that spoke to me where I am now in my life. It was one of those things of, “I guess I’ll just have to write it myself.”

articles.title_orig: MAGA Inc. plots final midterm money moves
articles.title_zh: MAGA Inc. plots final midterm money moves
articles.content_orig:
Political action committees supporting Republican Senate candidates have reported hundreds of millions of dollars in outside spending as the 2026 midterm elections approach, with major funds targeting key races across the country while President Donald Trump’s political operation has kept a large reserve of cash.
According to Legis1, the Senate Leadership Fund reported $173,991,698.46 in spending, directing opposition efforts across nine Senate contests. Ohio received $41.98 million, followed by North Carolina with $30.23 million and Michigan with $27.4 million.
The Senate Leadership Fund described its role in protecting the Republican Senate majority by saying, "it is the first line of defense to protect or Republican Senate majority." said SLF PAC, the Senate-focused political action committee.
Legis1 reported that Texas PAC ranked second with $133.56 million in cumulative outside spending, all focused on the Texas U.S. Senate contest. The group reported $68.82 million in support spending and $64.74 million in opposition spending.
The Texas Senate race has attracted $139.18 million in combined reported outside spending from the three largest PACs mentioned by Legis1. The general election is scheduled for Nov. 3, 2026, and the contest is rated a toss-up.
No Going Back PAC Inc., aligned with Trump’s movement, ranked third with $128,265,960.25 in reported spending. Its largest opposition expenditures targeted Ohio at $17.58 million, Michigan at $16.56 million and North Carolina at $8.73 million, according to Legis1.
MS NOW reported that Trump’s MAGA Inc. super PAC accumulated more than $400 million over the summer but has spent cautiously ahead of the midterms. The group reportedly began booking about $140 million in advertising through affiliated super PACs in mid-September after Republican officials sought more support.
A Trump aide explained the strategy by telling Time, "He wants to have as much money in his account as possible when he’s no longer able to raise the kind of money he can now," said a Trump aide.
The aide’s comments came amid discussion of whether Trump was prioritizing future political influence over immediate midterm spending. The same aide added, "He doesn’t seem to care that much about the midterms, thinks they’re a lost cause anyway, and wants to preserve future possibilities." said a Trump aide.
MS NOW reported that maintaining congressional control would affect Trump’s ability to advance legislation, appoint judges and respond to potential investigations. The report also noted that Trump’s fundraising capacity while in office could influence how he manages political resources after leaving office.

articles.title_orig: IT'S BACK. THAT'S BIG. The All-Electric smart #2 Makes Its World Premiere at the Paris Motor Show
articles.title_zh: IT'S BACK. THAT'S BIG. The All-Electric smart #2 Makes Its World Premiere at the Paris Motor Show
articles.content_orig:
HANGZHOU, China , Oct. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- smart today celebrated the World Premiere of the all-new smart #2 at the Paris Motor Show, marking the return of its iconic two-seater for a new electric era.
Thirty years ago, the smart vehicle was presented as an art object beneath the Louvre Pyramid. Today, smart returns to Paris with the fully realised production smart #2.
Mr. Tong Xiangbei, Global CEO of smart, said: "The smart #2 is more than the return of a familiar silhouette; it is a demonstration of what our teams can achieve in the most demanding urban segment. Its World Premiere in Paris, followed by launches in Europe and China, opens an important new chapter for our global product family."
Mr. Kang Yi, Global CMO of smart, said: "The smart #2 expresses our core D.N.A. in a very pure way: Designed with Love, No Compromise on Safety, and Amazing Drives. It is small in footprint, but big in personality."
An Icon for a New Generation
Styled by the Mercedes-Benz Global Design Team, the smart #2 translates the character of smart's iconic two-seater into a contemporary new form, guided by its design philosophy of Love, Pure, Unexpected.
Clean proportions, short overhangs and its signature wheels-at-the-corners stance preserve the pure smart silhouette and maximise space. Unexpected details, including logo-inspired lighting and a contemporary interpretation of the iconic floating roof, reinterpret familiar smart cues.
Inside, bench-style seating and S-shaped cockpit make efficient use of the compact cabin, while carefully considered colours, materials and distinctive details bring warmth and individuality.
The Split Tailgate features an upper glass that opens independently in tight spaces, and a lower section that folds down as a loading platform or a 120-kg capacity seat.
smart #2 Couture Edition: Function becomes Fashion
As a surprise highlight, smart also unveiled the exclusive smart #2 Couture Edition, carrying the established "Function becomes Fashion" theme from concept to production.
Limited to 999 units in Europe and 999 units in China, the Couture Edition combines an Atelier White Matte exterior finish with a contrasting Platinum Gold roof, distinctive gold detailing and exclusive 16-inch Lyra rims. A numbered interior badge further underlines its limited-edition character.
Purpose-Built for Urban Mobility
Underpinning the smart #2 is the newly developed Electric Compact Architecture (ECA) platform, engineered specifically for smart's ultra-compact all-electric two-seater.
Measuring 2,746 mm in length, the smart #2 maximises usable space within its ultra-compact footprint. The ECA platform brings together intelligent packaging, a floor-mounted high-voltage battery, rear-wheel drive and advanced chassis technology.
Power comes from a rear-mounted 60 kW electric motor delivering 130 Nm of torque to the rear wheels.
For Europe, the smart #2 features a 35.8 kWh LFP battery, with a target combined WLTP range of 290 km. Supporting 65 kW DC fast charging, the smart #2 can charge from 10% to 80% state of charge within 20 minutes, while AC charging at up to 11 kW supports convenient everyday charging.
A curb-to-curb turning circle of just 6.95 metres makes navigating tight city streets and narrow parking spaces effortless.
The smart #2 features a five-link rear suspension, a first in its class, supporting confident and composed driving both in cities and on highways.
Central to the smart #2, the Tridion Cell Evo creates a robust protective structure around the passenger cabin without compromising the vehicle's compact dimensions. The vehicle also comes equipped with driver-assistance technologies including smart Pilot Assist and Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC) with Stop & Go and Highway Assist.
The smart #2 Begins Its Global Market Rollout
Following its World Premiere in Paris, early ordering for the smart #2 will begin in Europe and China, bringing smart's iconic two-seater to two of the brand's key markets.
For Europe, the smart #2 will initially be offered in three core trim lines — Pure, Pure+ and Premium — alongside the limited Couture Edition.
For China, the smart #2 will be unveiled in Premium and Couture Edition variants.
Market-specific line-ups, pricing, specifications, equipment and availability will be communicated locally.

articles.title_zh: Russell Brand arrives at a London court for his trial on rape and sexual assault charges
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — Comedian Russell Brand arrived at a London court Monday for the opening of his trial on charges of rape and sexual assault.
Brand was flanked by security guards and accompanied by his wife, Laura Gallacher, as he arrived at Southwark Crown Court for the first day of a trial that is expected to last 10 to 12 weeks.
Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault. The offenses relate to six women and are alleged to have taken place between 1999 and 2009.
He has remained free on bail ahead of his trial.
Prosecutors have said at previous hearings that Brand is accused of raping a woman in a hotel room at a Labour Party conference, grabbing a TV worker’s breasts and forcing her into a sex act in a toilet, and kissing and groping a radio station worker.
Known for risque stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand was a major star of the early 2000s, with TV hosting jobs, his own BBC radio show and roles in films including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek.”
In recent years he has dropped out of mainstream media, moved to Florida and built a large following online with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.

articles.title_orig: Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports
articles.title_zh: Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports
articles.content_orig:
Saudi Arabia's energy minister has vowed a "serious" response to the deadly attacks on the kingdom's airports and oil and gas facilities by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement.
"The events of recent weeks are serious. Our response must be equally serious," Prince Abdul Aziz bin Salman told the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh.
On Sunday, a Pakistani man was killed in an attack on a terminal at the capital's King Khalid International Airport, Saudi authorities said. It came a day after a Houthi missile hit another terminal, killing 13 people and forcing its closure.
The Houthis said they launched the attacks in retaliation for "brutal Saudi aggression" against areas they control in western Yemen.
The Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six other people were injured in a Saudi air strike on a home in the capital, Sanaa, on Sunday.
A Saudi-led coalition is providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces battling the Houthis on Yemen's Red Sea coast and other areas.
The WPC Energy Congress opened on Sunday at a convention centre about 10km (6 miles) from Riyadh's airport, which has been attacked four times over the past week.
Last Thursday, three Saudis, including a pilot for the national airline Saudia, were killed in two strikes on an airport facility and an aircraft on the ground.
Another four Saudis, as well as two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian, one Sudanese and one Indian, were killed in Saturday's missile strike on Terminal 3.
On Sunday, a Pakistani resident was killed when a projectile hit Terminal 4, according to the General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).
King Fahd International Airport in the north-eastern city of Dammam was also attacked on Sunday evening, it said, but no casualties were reported.
Later, the Saudi-led coalition said its forces had intercepted a drone in Eastern Province and a missile launched by the Houthis towards the south-western city of Khamis Mushait.
In his inaugural address to the WPC Energy Congress on Monday, Prince Abdul Aziz thanked industry executives and policymakers for attending despite the attacks.
"You know this country is safe and that we hold your protection at whole heart," he said.
But he also acknowledged that "energy security cannot be taken for granted" and that recent developments had "tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people, and our resilience".
Prince Abdul Aziz promised that his country would overcome those challenges.
"We, as Saudis, are fearless, combatant and determined people," he said. "We shall prove it to the world that whatever we are going through we will overcome it."
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.
On Sunday evening, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said in a video statement that its forces had launched missiles and drones at Riyadh and Dammam's airports, as well as two oil and gas facilities in Eastern Province, in response to 124 Saudi air strikes in Yemen over the previous 24 hours.
Sarea also reiterated a warning to airlines and passengers against using Saudi airports and airspace, except for journeys to and from the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
The Houthis' forces, he vowed, would "continue their escalating operations deep inside Saudi, imposing the equation of 'a blockade for a blockade' and 'an escalation for an escalation' and targeting Saudi enemy reinforcements until the aggression ceases and the siege on our dear people is lifted".
Saturday's attack on Riyadh airport drew widespread international condemnation.
UN Secretary General António Guterres said he was "deeply shocked" and warned that attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure were a violation of international law.
President Donald Trump said he would "make a decision" about the US joining Saudi Arabia's strikes on the Houthis. The US military is reportedly already providing intelligence and targeting support to the Saudi-led coalition.
Iran, which has repeatedly denied allegations that it provides weapons and training to the Houthis, said it was "deeply concerned" by the escalation and called for "dialogue and engagement" to resolve the situation.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The Yemeni government claimed it was behind that strike, saying it was trying to prevent an unauthorised Iranian plane from landing.
Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea.
They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.
However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports after the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
Last week, the Yemeni government announced the start of a new offensive aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis.
Pro-government forces said they were quickly able to retake areas around Bab al-Mandab with the help of intense Saudi air strikes, but the Houthis denied losing any territory.

articles.title_zh: Productivity gains from AI could help offset Asia's ageing population problem, IMF says
articles.content_orig:
AI investment is propping up global growth amid energy shocks, but leaders at the IMF summit warn of a job tsunami threatening Asia’s youth
Soaring energy prices, persistent inflation and mounting debt framed the opening of the week-long summit, which was last hosted in the Thai capital in 1991.
Unusually, the US has not sent its Treasury Secretary to attend the gathering, despite triggering the energy crunch following its war against Iran, taken alongside Israel, in February.
Since then, oil prices have oscillated around US$100 a barrel thanks to the partial closure of the Strait of Hormuz, driving up inflation and forcing governments to drain reserves or borrow heavily to cushion consumers from high costs.

articles.title_orig: Giant pumpkins battle for heavyweight glory and the world record in California - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Giant pumpkins battle for heavyweight glory and the world record in California - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Giant pumpkin growers are gathering in Northern California for an annual pumpkin-weighing contest
HALF MOON BAY, Calif. -- Giant pumpkin growers and their massive gourds will converge on Monday in Northern California for an annual pumpkin-weighing contest, competing for the top prize and a chance to challenge the world record set just last week in England.
At least 30 growers of giant pumpkins have signed up for the 53rd World Championship Pumpkin Weigh-Off in Half Moon Bay, south of San Francisco, said event spokesman Ronan Fowler.
Among the participants is four-time champion Travis Gienger, a horticulture teacher from Minnesota, whose winning streak ended last year after he was unable to participate because his pumpkin broke while it was still growing.
Gienger, who this year had to deal with temperatures that dipped below freezing, grew a pumpkin whose circumference is so big it could be a world record contender, Fowler said.
Fowler said last week that Gienger and his father would take turns driving 30 hours over the weekend to get the pumpkin the size of a small car to California.
The new world record was set by Ian Paton, of Lymington, on England's south coast, with a giant squash weighing 2,857 pounds (1,296 kilograms). That's heavier than two and a half concert grand pianos .
Paton grows his giant gourds in a greenhouse, while Gienger grows them in the pumpkin patch in his backyard in Anoka, a city on the banks of the Mississippi River north of Minneapolis, Fowler said.
“The fact that Travis can weather the elements, like 30-degree weather, and still grow this massive pumpkin is pretty unbelievable,” the spokesman said.
Brandon Dawson, of Santa Rosa, California, who won the top prize last year with a behemoth of a pumpkin weighing 2,346 pounds (1,064 kilograms), will also compete.
The pumpkin champ this year will win $9 per pound of pumpkin and have their lumpy gourd showcased during a parade through Half Moon Bay this weekend. If they break the world record, they will take an extra prize of $30,000.
Monday’s festivities, which will kick off the city's fall celebration, will also include a special appearance by pumpkin carver Mike Valladao.
Sadly, these giants are grown for their size, not flavor, so there will be no giant pumpkin pies at the end of the festival.
Rodriguez reported from San Francisco.

articles.title_orig: Huawei in collaboration with China Unicom and Peking University Win 2026 Leading Lights Award, Advancing 5G Free-Mobility Private Network to a New Era in Higher Education
articles.title_zh: Huawei in collaboration with China Unicom and Peking University Win 2026 Leading Lights Award, Advancing 5G Free-Mobility Private Network to a New Era in Higher Education
articles.content_orig:
Light Reading, the globally recognized authority in communications industry media, has announced the winners of its 22nd Leading Lights Awards. The " Peking University CARSI 5G Free-Mobility Private Network " jointly submitted by Huawei, China Unicom, and Peking University, stood out among 151 shortlisted projects worldwide, winning the Outstanding Use Case: Network Security & Resilience Use Case Award. This recognition marks a new chapter in the application of 5G private networks within the higher education sector. As AI-driven research and digital campus life accelerate across universities, faculty and students are placing greater demands on campus networks. Previously, access to internal campus resources relied on the traditional internet + VPN model. This approach carries security risks, including data leakage and account compromises. It also delivers a poor user experience, with high latency, unstable connections, and repeated login prompts. These shortcomings no longer meet the needs of modern universities. At the same time, conventional 5G private networks suffer from lengthy service provisioning cycles and elevated management costs. They are ill-suited to the high personnel turnover typical of academic institutions. Breaking through the security and experience bottlenecks of traditional VPN models  and enabling faculty and students to access campus resources securely and conveniently from anywhere outside campus  has become a shared priority in university IT modernization. In response, Huawei and China Unicom have jointly introduced the " Peking University CARSI 5G Free-Mobility Private Network " solution  directly addressing the security risks and experience gaps faced by faculty and students accessing campus intranet resources from off-campus locations. The solution delivers a seamless upgrade in campus resource access: no VPN cluster, no annual licence planning, no SIM approval workflow. Zero-Touch Onboarding: Built on CARSI (Campus Authentication and Resource Sharing Infrastructure), the federated authentication system of CERNET (China Education and Research Network), faculty and students can activate the 5G Mobile Private Network using their existing university credentials. A single phone  without changing SIM cards or phone numbers  provides seamless access to the campus network, eliminating the need to install or repeatedly start and stop VPN clients.
Light Reading judges commented: This architecture  The university, not the operator, remains the sole identity authority  carries significant replication potential. The solution leverages the existing CERNET infrastructure without requiring large-scale campus network modernization, and can be rapidly deployed across the universities already connected to CARSI. The 5G Free-Mobility Private Network is now officially live at Peking University, covering the core scenario of off-campus access to campus intranet resources. Faculty and students enjoy seamless campus network access with a single phone  no SIM change, no number change. During a three-month pilot involving over 100 faculty and students, more than 70% of respondents rated the new service as superior to traditional VPNs in stability, latency, and ease of use. Service provisioning time was reduced from several days to seconds, and the private network deployment cycle was compressed from approximately three months to three weeks. This solution provides a replicable model for 5G private network deployment across the universities connected to CARSI, with the potential for international extension. Looking ahead, Huawei will continue to deepen joint innovation with China Unicom across more universities  focusing on 5G-Advanced, 6G, network security, and AI-native networks (AIDN)  to advance the network-as-a-service vision in the education sector. By helping quality educational resources transcend campus boundaries, Huawei is committed to contributing a China-based solution and Chinas wisdom to global university digital transformation. FAQs: Q1: What is CARSI? CARSI (Campus Authentication and Resource Sharing Infrastructure) is a unified identity authentication platform built by CERNET (China Education and Research Network). It now covers over 1,000 universities across China, enabling cross-institutional identity mutual recognition and resource sharing. Q2: What problem does the 5G Mobile Private Network solve? Traditionally, faculty and students must install VPN clients to access campus intranet resources  a process that introduces security risks and delivers a frustrating experience. With the 5G Free-Mobility Private Network, users reach the campus network seamlessly through China Unicoms 5G service. No new SIM card, no number change, no additional setup is needed. The system also resolves the management overhead caused by frequent faculty turnover and the continuous cycle of student enrollment and graduation, automatically terminating access when users leave the university. Q3: What application scenarios does the 5G Mobile Private Network currently support? The 5G Mobile Private Network is now officially live at Peking University, enabling faculty and students to access campus intranet resources using 5G data from off-campus locations. In the future, this solution can be rapidly replicated across the more than 1,000 universities connected to CARSI, and can extend to overseas universities through eduGAIN.

articles.title_orig: Astronomers discover possible second-generation planet formed from dying star junk
articles.title_zh: Astronomers discover possible second-generation planet formed from dying star junk
articles.content_orig:
Scientists discovered first-of-its-kind evidence of a possible second-generation planet around a white dwarf star some 270 light years away from Earth.
Astronomers found chemical signatures that indicated that gases cast off from the dead star HS 0209+0832 had coalesced into an alien world roughly the size of Jupiter, according to a study published last week in Nature Astronomy .
A team of UK-based scientists took a second look at data garnered from NASA’s Hubble Telescope in 1999 and noted about 100 unidentified chemical features around the dense dead star, which is located in the Milky Way and can be seen in the constellation Cetus.
Researchers theorized that the discovery of abundant “astronomically special” elements like niobium and other elements heavier than iron suggest that a planet had been formed and HS 0209+0832 had been feeding off it.
The experts believe that the planet was formed from stellar material ejected from the white dwarf as it dies. In contrast, most planets — like those in our solar system — are created when a star is born.
“These heavy elements can only be synthesized in the exotic conditions that briefly emerge inside dying stars,”  Dr. Nicholas Stone, a theoretical astrophysicist at the University of Wisconsin – Madison and study co-author, told Sci.News .
Scientists also found a repeating brightness cycle of about 4.4 days, which could line up with the day and night temperature variation of a massive planet orbiting very close to its star — at .04 Astronomical Units, or 25 times closer than the Earth is to the Sun.
If the purported planet exists, it was losing atmosphere, but researchers were hopeful about its fate.
“If the second-generation planet is there, I think it is likely to survive,” University of Warwick astronomer and study co-author Jamie Williams said, according to the article.
“Eventually the white dwarf will cool and then maintain a consistent temperature, with the planet in its stable habitable zone for millions of years.”
The steady temperature could mean a close-in rocky planet could remain habitable for tens of billions of year, far longer than Earth which will be engulfed or burned by the Sun when it dies within 5 billion years, Williams noted to Universe Today .
The discovery of the first-ever second generation planet had yet to be officially verified and more research was needed, experts said.

articles.title_orig: Around the World in Explorer Names
articles.title_zh: Around the World in Explorer Names
articles.content_orig:
At the Explorers Club, uptown, the American Geographical Society, founded in 1851, celebrated its hundred-and-seventy-fifth year one recent evening by observing its most sacred ritual: a ceremonial globe signing. The society’s Fliers & Explorers Globe, donated in 1929 by the Times editor and A.G.S. president John Finley, was signed by many of his era’s most renowned explorers, including Charles Lindbergh, Amelia Earhart, and Sir Edmund Hillary. “Finley interviewed people who came in from their expeditions, and he’d get them to sign it,” Jerome Dobson, an A.G.S. president emeritus, said. His necktie had an antique-map print. Later, the globe was signed by John Glenn, Neil Armstrong, the Apollo 8 crew, and others. That night, it would be signed by the oceanographer, former Navy captain, and retired astronaut Kathryn Sullivan—the first person to both walk in outer space and visit the deepest point of the ocean, in the Mariana Trench.
During cocktail hour, a spiffily dressed group of eminent geographers gathered in the library bar around a Fliers & Explorers replica—a party globe, perhaps. “This is the globe you can touch,” Marie Price, the current A.G.S. president, said. “Spin it around!” (“Let’s not go wild,” Dobson said.) The library had an icy-exploration theme: taxidermied polar bear, signed Shackleton portrait, Admiral Peary’s ice pick, snowy painting of bedraggled men by a tent. “That looks like one of our camp trips, huh, Lee?” Price said to Lee Schwartz, a former GOTUS (Geographer of the United States).
When Dobson joined A.G.S., in 1997, the Fliers & Explorers Globe was underappreciated, he said. “I didn’t even notice it,” he recalled. “It was on a spindly shaft in the corner; we’d go spin it.” It hadn’t seen much action since Glenn had signed it, at the White House, in front of J.F.K., Lyndon Johnson, “and two of Bobby Kennedy’s children—not the one currently in government.” Seeing an opportunity, Dobson had proposed new signings. “Who wouldn’t consider it an honor?” he said. “So we invited Neil Armstrong; Don Walsh and Jacques Piccard, the first people to go to the bottom of the Mariana Trench; and Bertrand Piccard and Brian Jones, who first circumnavigated the globe in a balloon.” (Were the Piccards inspiration for Captain Picard, of “Star Trek”? “I never thought of that,” Price said.) The retired Coast Guard captain Lawson Brigham, who resembled a seafaring Lee Iacocca, approached the globe. “I signed through the Bering Strait, but I had been at the North Pole and the South Pole,” he said, pointing. “As close to the South Pole as you get on a Coast Guard icebreaker.”
“Lawson did the circumnavigation pole to pole, not the most common way to go,” Price said. “You need an icebreaker.” (“There is a precedent—names on here of pilots who went that way,” Dobson said.) Nearby, wearing a waterproof modern-adventurer hat, the eighty-five-year-old G.P.S. pioneer Charlie Trimble chatted about trying to determine whether Mt. Everest was rising or sinking. (Rising, he said.)
During the main event, in a ballroom, Sullivan, a capable-looking seventy-five-year-old with a blond bob and a dark jacket and slacks, approached the globe, accepted a Sharpie, and said, “Right under my very good friend and shipmate Don Walsh.” People craned their necks. A partygoer whispered, “Where do you sign the globe if you’re an astronaut?”
Afterward, Sullivan retired to the terrace. Deep-sea exploration, she said, “is not a bad analogue for going into space.” Both require a vehicle “that can take your squishy little body to a place that it clearly doesn’t belong. I’m comfortable inside, and I look through a window and know that right out there I would die. How is it possible for me to be here, eating my tuna-fish sandwich?” She went to Challenger Deep, the bottom of the trench, in 2020. “The word that kept coming to mind was ‘moonscape,’ ” she said. “A fine, silty sediment, gently rolling bottom, a little more tan than the gray of the moon”; barren, to our eyes, with “typically unsexy critters like burrowing worms.” As for space, “It’s a very dramatic experience, getting off the planet,” she said. “You’re basically riding a bomb for eight and a half minutes. And then you have the magical experience of being effectively weightless, maneuvering and living and working in zero gravity, which is great, great, great fun. And the view is stupendous.” Her crews’ data collection would seem tedious to outside observers, she said, but on one mission, “we deployed the Hubble Space Telescope.” Many of the people whose signatures appear on the globe had been meaningful to her (Earhart, Walsh, Armstrong, “the whole Apollo 8 crew”); as a kid, she’d admired astronauts and Jacques Cousteau. “These were people living inquisitive and adventurous lives,” she said. “I wanted my life to be like that.” ♦

articles.title_orig: UK's Burnham accuses Russia of meddling in Brexit vote
articles.title_zh: UK's Burnham accuses Russia of meddling in Brexit vote
articles.content_orig:
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Sunday became the first British leader to openly complain of Russian tampering in the Brexit referendum a decade ago.
Burnham, who took on the role in July from Keir Starmer, thinks leaving the European Union did "more harm than good" and has opened the door to closer ties, including possibly rejoining the bloc.
Burnham told The Rest Is Politics podcast that he had posed the question upon first arriving in Downing Street, and was given a "clear answer that yes, there was [a link to Russian interference]."
He did not provide evidence of the Kremlin's efforts to influence the June 2016 vote, where the UK decided to leave the EU by a 52% to 48% majority .
With the rise of far-right parties in the UK and across the EU, Burnham ​said voters needed better information about efforts by rogue states to disrupt their democracies.
"These things are important now to put clearly on the ​record, and I believe, ‌help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia," he said.
Burnham described how German Chancellor Friedrich Merz had told him during talks in Berlin this week that the AfD is "clearly linked to Russia — funded, I believe.”
"There is certainly misinformation, disinformation that is emanating from Russia into German politics,” Burnham added.
Burnham's Brexit remarks contrast with former Prime Minister Boris Johnson, who campaigned to leave the EU. In 2020, Johnson said ​there was no evidence of Russian sway.
The UK Parliament’s Intelligence and Security Committee found in 2020 that the government had failed to fully assess how Russian state-run media and “troll” accounts could have impacted the vote.
In its report, the Committee also found the Kremlin sought to influence Scotland's 2014 independence referendum, which was rejected by voters.
The UK's intelligence agencies believe Russia continues to spread disinformation to undermine public trust, alongside cyberattacks, sabotage and espionage . They say the issue is getting worse and is often aided by artificial intelligence (AI).
Russia has long denied meddling in other countries' elections or referendums.
After the Brexit vote, it cast some British politicians as gripped by anti-Russian hysteria.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Polling firm YouGov runs a regular tracker on whether the UK was right or wrong to vote to quit.
Since mid-2022, a majority of people surveyed said Britain was wrong to leave. Last month, the "Bregret" camp rose to 60% — the highest ever.
Last month, Burnham said he would seek a political consensus on the country's future relationship with the EU, even suggesting he could campaign to take Britain back into the bloc at the next election.
EU officials have welcomed the change in tone from London, while France and Spain have spoken positively about closer ties, including rejoining.
Some experts remain skeptical, however. Professor Iain Begg of the London School of Economics thinks rejoining would reopen deep political divisions, be complicated from both the EU and UK sides and likely take years.
