articles.title_orig: Scientists find hidden driver of aging and a simple amino acid that fights memory loss in mice
articles.title_zh: Scientists find hidden driver of aging and a simple amino acid that fights memory loss in mice
articles.content_orig:
What if some of the changes we associate with aging begin with the loss of a single protein deep inside the brain? Scientists investigating that possibility found that restoring a protein called Menin in older mice improved memory, balance, bone mass, and skin thickness in just 30 days. Even more surprisingly, supplementing the animals with a naturally occurring amino acid improved their learning and memory in only three weeks.
The findings, originally published in March 2023 in PLOS Biology , came from researchers led by Lige Leng of Xiamen University in China. Their experiments identified a previously overlooked connection between inflammation, brain chemistry, and aging throughout the body. Although the results were obtained in mice, they raised an intriguing possibility: Some effects of aging may be influenced by biological processes in the brain that scientists could eventually learn to modify.
Research published since then has added evidence that the brain plays an important role in regulating aging. It has also revealed why the seemingly simple supplement findings deserve careful interpretation.
How a Hidden Brain Protein May Influence Aging
At the center of the discovery is the hypothalamus, a small but powerful region near the base of the brain. It helps regulate essential functions such as body temperature, hunger, metabolism, sleep, and hormone production. Because these systems affect nearly every organ, changes in the hypothalamus can have consequences throughout the body.
Scientists have increasingly recognized the hypothalamus as an important player in aging. One possible reason involves neuroinflammation, the brain's inflammatory response. Although inflammation helps protect against infections and injuries, persistent inflammation can interfere with normal cellular function and contribute to age-related deterioration.
Earlier work by Leng and colleagues had identified Menin as a protein that helps restrain inflammation in the hypothalamus. Menin also participates in regulating gene activity, allowing it to influence multiple biological pathways.
The researchers wanted to understand what happens when this protective protein begins to disappear with age.
They discovered that Menin levels gradually declined in certain hypothalamic neurons as mice grew older. Interestingly, the same decrease was not observed in astrocytes or microglia, two other important types of brain cells involved in supporting neurons and managing immune responses.
To investigate whether this decline actually contributed to aging, the team developed genetically modified mice in which Menin could be selectively disabled.
The results were striking. Mice with reduced Menin activity developed greater inflammation in the hypothalamus, thinner skin, reduced bone mass, and worsening cognitive performance. Their lifespans were also modestly shortened.
Rather than simply accompanying aging, the loss of Menin appeared capable of helping drive several of its characteristic changes.
Restoring Menin Reversed Several Signs of Aging in 30 Days
The researchers then asked an even more interesting question: If declining Menin contributes to aging, could restoring the protein reverse some of the damage?
To find out, they used a gene delivery technique to increase Menin production in a specific part of the hypothalamus in older (20-month-old) mice. This region, called the ventromedial hypothalamus, helps coordinate metabolism, energy balance, and other bodily functions.
Just 30 days after treatment, the animals showed measurable improvements.
Their skin became thicker, bone mass increased, and performance improved on tests measuring learning, memory, and balance. Researchers also observed reductions in inflammation and improvements in certain metabolic changes associated with aging.
In a separate survival analysis, mice receiving the Menin treatment also lived longer than untreated controls.
These findings suggested that some biological changes associated with old age could be at least partially reversed by restoring Menin activity in a specific group of brain cells.
But the researchers also uncovered an important clue about how Menin produced these effects.
A Simple Amino Acid Offers a Surprising Clue
When Menin levels declined, the researchers noticed that concentrations of D-serine, an amino acid involved in brain signaling, also fell.
Amino acids are best known as the building blocks of proteins, but some perform other important functions. D-serine helps regulate NMDA receptors, specialized proteins on nerve cells that are essential for communication between neurons, learning, and the formation of memories.
D-serine is closely related to L-serine, an amino acid commonly found in foods such as soybeans, eggs, fish, and nuts. The two forms have different biological roles. Although D-serine is also available as a dietary supplement, consuming ordinary serine-rich foods is not equivalent to taking the form used in the experiments.
Further investigation revealed that Menin helps control the production of PHGDH, an enzyme involved in the biochemical pathway that generates serine (which was in turn regulated by Menin). When Menin activity decreased, this pathway became less active, reducing the amount of D-serine available to the brain.
Restoring Menin increased D-serine levels in the hippocampus, a region especially important for learning and memory.
This connection suggested that the cognitive effects of declining Menin might be partly explained by disruptions in D-serine signaling.
To test the idea directly, the scientists gave older mice D-serine in their drinking water for three weeks.
The supplementation improved their performance on learning and memory tests, even without directly restoring Menin.
However, there was an important distinction. While increasing Menin improved both cognitive function and physical signs of aging, D-serine supplementation primarily improved cognition. It did not restore the age-related losses in bone mass and skin thickness.
That difference suggests Menin influences aging through several biological mechanisms, with D-serine accounting for only part of its effects.
Later Research Strengthens the Link Between the Brain and Aging
Since the original 2023 discovery, additional studies have provided evidence that the hypothalamus helps coordinate aging across the body.
In a 2024 study published in Cell Metabolism , researchers at Washington University School of Medicine identified a different group of hypothalamic neurons that communicates with fat tissue. By maintaining or stimulating this communication pathway, they increased physical activity, improved age-related metabolic function, and extended lifespan in mice.
That work involved a different protein and neural circuit from Menin, but supported the broader idea that signals originating in the hypothalamus can influence how the rest of the body ages.
Another 2024 study in the Journal of Physiology and Biochemistry provided additional insight into Menin itself. Researchers found that increasing Menin helped protect cultured hippocampal cells against inflammation and a form of programmed cell death triggered by exposure to the stress hormone corticosterone. Although these laboratory experiments did not establish an anti-aging effect, they supported the idea that Menin has important protective functions in brain cells.
An even larger picture emerged in January 2025, when scientists published a detailed analysis of approximately 1.2 million mouse brain cells in Nature .
The researchers discovered that some of the brain cells most sensitive to aging were concentrated around the third ventricle, a fluid-filled cavity in the hypothalamus. Many aging cells showed reduced activity in genes involved in normal neuronal function and increased activity in genes associated with inflammation and immune responses.
These findings highlighted the hypothalamus as a potential center of vulnerability during brain aging, althou

articles.title_orig: Final MINT Study Results Strengthen Real-World Evidence for Mogamulizumab (Poteligeo®) in Patients With Mycosis Fungoides and Sézary Syndrome
articles.title_zh: Final MINT Study Results Strengthen Real-World Evidence for Mogamulizumab (Poteligeo®) in Patients With Mycosis Fungoides and Sézary Syndrome
articles.content_orig:
GALASHIELS, Scotland & MARLOW, England--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Kyowa Kirin International plc, a wholly owned subsidiary of Kyowa Kirin Co., Ltd. (TSE:4151, Kyowa Kirin), today announced final results from the German MINT study evaluating mogamulizumab in patients with mycosis fungoides (MF) and Sézary Syndrome (SS). Presented at the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer Cutaneous Lymphoma Tumour Group (EORTC-CLTG) Annual Meeting 2026 in Berlin, Germany, the findings represent one of the largest real-world evaluations of mogamulizumab in Germany and add to the growing body of evidence supporting its use in routine clinical practice. 1-3
Conducted as a company-sponsored, multicentric, non-interventional, combined retro-prospective real-world study across 18 centres throughout Germany, MINT brought together cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma (CTCL) specialists to evaluate treatment outcomes with mogamulizumab in a real-world setting, with time-to-next-treatment (TTNT) as the study’s primary endpoint. 1 The study captured a broad and heterogeneous patient population, including clinically relevant subgroups such as patients with large cell transformation (LCT) and folliculotropic mycosis fungoides (fMF), and stratified by disease stage and mogamulizumab-associated rash (MAR) status, providing insights that complement evidence generated through controlled clinical studies. 1,4
MF and SS are forms of CTCL, a type of non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma that manifests on the skin, 5 though the disease can also involve the blood, lymph nodes and visceral organs. 6 Symptoms can include persistent, itchy and scaly rashes, changes in skin colour and patches, plaques and/or tumours. 7 These visible and often difficult-to-hide symptoms can make everyday activities harder and significantly affect patients’ quality of life, including their work, relationships and social lives, 8 and for some patients the disease can progress to affect long-term survival. 9
“For patients living with mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome, understanding how treatments perform outside the controlled setting of clinical trials is critically important. The final MINT results demonstrate meaningful clinical outcomes across a broad patient population treated in routine practice and highlight the value of collaborative real-world research in helping clinicians make informed treatment decisions,” said Professor Chalid Assaf, Director of the Department of Dermatology and Venereology, Helios Klinikum Krefeld, Health and Medical University Düsseldorf-Krefeld, Germany.
The final analysis included 109 patients, comprising 56 patients with MF and 53 patients with SS, with a median follow-up of 25.2 months. 1 The majority of patients had advanced disease when they started treatment, with 83.5% at stage IIB or above. 1 The study demonstrated durable treatment outcomes, reporting a median TTNT of 14.9 months, a best overall response rate of 62.4%, and an overall median progression-free survival of 20.2 months. 1 Median overall survival was not estimable at the time of analysis due to the limited number of deaths observed, despite up to 71 months of follow-up in some cases. 1
Looking more closely at treatment response in clinically relevant patient subgroups, exploratory analyses reported best overall response rates of 54.5% in patients with LCT (n=11; 95% CI: 23.4–83.3) and 50.0% in patients with fMF (n=12; 95% CI: 21.1–78.9). Additional exploratory analyses by disease stage showed best overall response rates of 50% in patients with early-stage disease (n=18; 95% CI: 26.0–74.0) and 64.8% in patients with advanced stage disease (n=91; 95% CI: 54.1–74.6). 10 Disease control rate was also reported in patients with MAR (n=47), at 95.7%. 4
TTNT is an important measure in real-world clinical practice as it reflects both disease control and the duration of clinical benefit before a patient requires an alternative treatment approach. The study reported a median TTNT of 12.0 months in patients with MF and 20.2 months in patients with SS. 4 Patients also experienced improvements in quality of life, with median Skindex-29 scores improving by 38.5% from 49.1 at treatment initiation (n=21) to 30.2 at Month 12 (n=7). 1
“MINT provides valuable real-world evidence from Germany on the use of mogamulizumab across the heterogeneous population of patients with mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome, including clinically relevant subgroups that are often underrepresented in clinical trials. By evaluating time-to-next-treatment as a clinically meaningful outcome, the study offers practical insights that can support CTCL specialists in making informed, individualised treatment decisions,” said Dr. Azeem Danish, Medical Affairs Director, DACH, Kyowa Kirin.
The investigators concluded that, in a real-world setting, mogamulizumab demonstrated a safety profile comparable to that observed in the pivotal Phase 3 MAVORIC study, while providing clinical benefits in treatment response and quality of life for patients with MF and SS. 1,5 Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events were reported in 38.5% of patients, most commonly drug eruption and lymphopenia. 1 Serious treatment-related adverse events leading to discontinuation occurred in 22.0% of patients. 1
Kyowa Kirin has supported the generation of real-world evidence in CTCL through collaborations with investigators and treatment centres across Europe. The MINT study contributes to a growing evidence base exploring outcomes in patients treated with mogamulizumab in routine clinical practice 1-3 and reflects a shared commitment between investigators and industry to advancing understanding of rare cancers and improving care for patients living with CTCL.
MINT (Mogamulizumab In a Non-interventional study to evaluate the safety and outcome in mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome Treatment) is a German multicentric, non-interventional, retro-prospective real-world study evaluating the effectiveness and tolerability of mogamulizumab in patients with mycosis fungoides (MF) and Sézary Syndrome (SS). Data were collected from patient medical records across 18 study sites in Germany. The primary endpoint was time-to-next-treatment, with secondary endpoints including response rate, progression-free survival, overall survival, quality of life and tolerability. 1
Kyowa Kirin aims to discover novel medicines with life-changing value. As a global specialty pharmaceutical company, we have invested in drug discovery and biotechnology innovation for more than 75 years and are currently working to engineer the next generation of antibodies and cell and gene therapies with the potential to help patients affected by severe and rare diseases. A shared commitment to our values, to sustainable growth, and to making people smile unites us across our three regions: JAPAC, North America, and EMEA.
You can learn more about the business of Kyowa Kirin at: https://kyowakirininternational.com/ .
About mycosis fungoides (MF) and Sézary Syndrome (SS)
MF and SS are two subtypes of cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma (CTCL), which is itself a rare form of non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma that presents and persists in the skin. 5 CTCL is treatable, but is not generally considered to be curable, and there has been a clear unmet need for novel treatment options. As well as the obvious impact of symptoms upon patients, there can be significant erosions to quality of life for those caring for an individual living with CTCL. 11
MF and SS are characterised by localisation of cancerous white blood cells called T lymphocytes (T cells), to the skin. 9 These cancerous T cells consistently express a protein called CCR4, which enables them to move from the blood to the skin. 12-14 When these cancerous T cells move to the skin, this results in the visible early skin symptoms of red patches or plaques which can resemble psoriasis or eczema in the early stages of the disease. 7 Later, for some patients, skin involvement may evolve to include tumo

articles.title_orig: Top oil executives dropped from event schedule after Riyadh attacks
articles.title_zh: Top oil executives dropped from event schedule after Riyadh attacks
articles.content_orig:
As Saudi Arabia reckons with the deadliest attack on its soil in more than a decade, questions swirl over how Riyadh will respond as Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis continue to wreak havoc on the kingdom.
The kingdom launched a major offensive last week to support Yemeni government forces fighting the Houthis, but the rebels have so far held their ground.
Instead, they have escalated their campaign against the kingdom, culminating in missile attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport over the weekend that killed at least 13 people.
Drawing from Iran’s playbook in its conflict with the United States, the Houthis are vowing a painful escalation, targeting critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and imposing a global economic cost.
The Houthis have longstanding grievances against Saudi Arabia over Riyadh’s decade-long war against the group, which triggered the world’s worst humanitarian crisis. The recent Houthi escalation, however, is increasingly seen as an extension of Iran’s conflict with Washington.
After eleven years of trying to contain the Houthi advance militarily and through talks, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and his brother, Defense Minister Khaled bin Salman, face limited options. Across the border, the rebels have grown more powerful, consolidating control over major cities and pushing to seize others, such as the densely populated Taiz.
“This threat has to be dealt with once and for all,” Ali Shihabi, an author and commentator on Saudi politics told CNN. “A lot will depend on the performance of the Yemeni government troops on the ground and Saudi is helping them extensively with air power.”
So far , Saudi Arabia has largely confined its role to providing air cover for the anti-Houthi Yemeni coalition, stopping short of any major deployment of its own troops on the ground. Whether that restraint will hold after Saturday’s strike on Riyadh remains an open question.
Sending large numbers of Saudi troops into Yemen would plunge the kingdom into a an expensive and grinding ground war across rugged terrain and undercut the image Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is carefully cultivating of a stable, investment-friendly kingdom and global tourism hub.
Barely two decades ago, the Houthis were little more than a small religious revivalist movement. With Iranian backing, they have since grown into a formidable fighting force in possession of ballistic missiles and capable of striking as far away as Tel Aviv.
“They’ve developed their warfare,” a southern Yemeni official who fought the Houthis for years told CNN. “They’ve gotten more sophisticated in their attacks, they’re persistent and they’ve enhanced their intelligence.”
Yemen’s government alleges that Houthi rebels have worked with Iranian Revolutionary Guard experts to modify missiles into more effective weapons.
The new missiles fly faster and use a thermal-tracking system to home in on any heat source, Majed al-Nazili, spokesperson for the Yemen’s armed forces, said. It remains unclear whether such missiles were used during Saturday’s attack on Riyadh airport.
The Houthis’ pursuit of more sophisticated weapons may now be extending into artificial intelligence.
AI company Anthropic said a group based in northern Yemen used its Claude AI tools to help develop guidance software for rockets and missiles – the systems that steer and stabilize the weapons in flight. The report did not identify those involved, but their location in Houthi-controlled northern Yemen suggests a possible link to the rebels.
Saudi Arabia has sought support from partners across the world to counter the group. France, Britain and Pakistan have committed support, while other allies like Turkey are considering sending help.
Prince Mohammed has also reportedly turned to Syria for help. Its president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, had led armed factions that successfully drove Iranian-backed groups from Syria after nearly a decade of civil war.
Yet Riyadh’s biggest ally, the US, has not supported air strikes on the Houthis, instead sending more than 100 military advisers to provide intelligence under a newly formed joint command.
Last year Washington reached a ceasefire with the Iran-backed group that reopened the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the maritime chokepoint through which global trade flows between Asia and Europe, to US vessels. Prince Mohammed spoke twice with Trump last month , urging him to strike the Houthis, sources told CNN at the time, but the president declined to intervene.
How a series of miscalculations restarted Saudi Arabia’s war in Yemen
“Clearly, direct US involvement via air power would help because US aircraft can respond to US satellite intelligence more rapidly,” Shihabi said. “Saudi aircraft… are one stop removed from that loop so US involvement would be helpful.”
Saudi Arabia, one of the largest countries in the Middle East, remains vulnerable despite procuring some of the most advanced US air defenses. Its infrastructure, which carries rich resources across vast desert terrain, leaves it an easy target for the cheaper one-way drones developed by the Houthis.
Among those killed in the Houthi attack on the Riyadh airport was an American citizen, the Saudi civil aviation body said Sunday – an attack that might draw Trump further into the war.
“The Saudis are good fighters,” Trump told reporters following the attack. “But I think the attack was a terrible thing.”
Asked whether the US will join strikes on the Houthis, the US president said: “We may”

articles.title_orig: A Swiss retired pastor witnesses the life reality in Lebanon
articles.title_zh: A Swiss retired pastor witnesses the life reality in Lebanon
articles.content_orig:
Rev. Serge Fornerod brings forty years of international experience in development, public administration and ecumenical relations. Following the fall of the Berlin Wall, he managed aid and development programmes in Eastern Europe and later contributed to international relations within the umbrella organisation for Switzerland’s Protestant Churches. Since retiring in 2023, he has remained active in ecumenical networks, supporting the Foundation for Aid to Reformed Protestantism and the John Knox International Reformed Centre in Geneva.
Rev. Fornerod is a former member of the World Council of Churches central committee. He is also involved in preparations for the 2027 Francophone Christian Forum and researches the spread of early Christianity, particularly in the East . He took time to reflect on a new blog he has created that documents his experience at the Near East School of Theology (NEST) in Beirut, and his thoughts on the key to Christian unity.
What inspired you to start your blog to document your experience at the Near East school of Theology in Beirut?
Rev. Fornerod: Through this blog, I ’ d like to share some reflections and convictions I have formed over the last few years within the ecumenical movement and in my personal life.
The first is that when a parent is unwell, seriously afflicted by illness for years on end, telling them – as I often read on social media from “ good Christians” and – sorry to say – even church leaders – “ we ’ re thinking of you” or “ our prayers are with you” only helps the person saying it. Potentially, such phrases eventually add to the parent ’ s suffering, leaving them feeling even more alone. Someone who is ill, someone in despair, someone rendered invisible and voiceless by misfortune and injustice – that is someone you visit. You must take the time to listen and truly understand what the other person is going through. I believe that the Christian West (in general) takes its responsibility towards situations of suffering in the world and the churches experiencing them far too lightly. If we truly believe that the faith and life of churches elsewhere in the world concern us directly, then we must talk less about “ solidarity” – when this has no impact on our daily lives – and take more action. "Witness is with-ness.”
The second message is that in the world of ecumenical relations or relations between churches, the key to unity is not primarily dialogue, but listening. In light of everything that has been happening in the Middle East for decades, but especially since October 2023, I wanted to come and listen to the voices of Christians on the ground. Back home in Switzerland – though I fear this may also be the case elsewhere – I had the impression that opinions were quickly set in stone regarding who the culprits and who the victims were. My limited experience of the Middle East so far has very quickly made me feel uncomfortable in the face of so many so-called certainties, which in fact conceal unacknowledged political and cultural preconceptions. I wanted to give more space to the concrete reality of people ’ s lives and the experiences of the churches here. To listen, one must step back from one ’ s own context; one must be prepared to remain silent for a long while; one must be prepared to place trust first and foremost in the person who is in that situation; and one must draw closer, physically as well. The NEST faculty, with its international and ecumenical identity—driven by young people and researchers rather than officials (whom I also meet frequently and with pleasure!)—strikes me as an ideal place for observation, networking, and gathering information.
What do you hope others gain from you sharing your learning pilgrimage?
Rev. Fornerod: I hope to raise awareness amongst as many readers as possible of the need to take the time to reflect and find out more before forming an opinion on what is happening in this region. But also to show that it is relatively easy to obtain insightful background information on people ’ s experiences and the living conditions under which people here must face these new challenges. Action is easily possible and effective. When you consult the local sources here, it is striking to see, for instance, how many people in Israel oppose the destruction campaign of the Israeli army and how many people in Lebanon are engaged in bringing help. And lastly to hear that, for the Christians here, there is quite simply no alternative but to hold their heads high and carry on fighting day in, day out for dignity and justice – whether in their personal lives, their country ’ s politics or international justice. And if there is a Westerner present at the gatherings where people pray for this here, then perhaps that might do a little good.
Can you describe the way in which you are engaging with people?
Rev. Fornerod: One of the very nice and positive aspects of “ just being here,” free enough to engage with people is indeed to see the ease, spontaneity, hospitality, and kindness with which the Lebanese respond to your presence, however surprised they might be. It is a life lesson to see that, in an international, national, economic, and social situation as complicated and desperate as the one here, people naturally manage to draw strength from and take pleasure in making you happy.

articles.title_orig: Facing smaller crowds and low approval ratings, Trump tries to rally the base for the midterms
articles.title_zh: Facing smaller crowds and low approval ratings, Trump tries to rally the base for the midterms
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
WASHINGTON — As President Trump zigzags across the country in the final weeks before the midterm elections, he has made California his favorite foil as he tries to fire up his base.
On Monday, he blamed the Golden State for the rising cost of gas prices, claimed without evidence that its elections are rigged, and at a Nebraska rally suggested Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego.
“It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe,” Trump said. “They can take out a city, let them take out Los Angeles, let them take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay.”
The president’s team on Tuesday said his remarks were misunderstood, arguing the president “clearly” stated that U.S. cities would have been threatened “if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped.” Trump declined to clarify what he meant by his statements when asked by a reporter  Tuesday.
But by then, Trump’s remarks had already drawn fierce condemnation from California leaders, including Republican Jim Desmond, a Navy veteran running in a highly competitive race that is key to helping Republicans retain control of the House.
“I vehemently disagree with President Trump’s comments,” Desmond wrote on social media. “America must stand up to Iran and defend our interests, but the first responsibility of our Commander in Chief is to protect the American people and our homeland.”
The backlash exposed the risk of Trump’s closing midterm strategy. Bashing California is a reliable applause line in red states like Nebraska, Alabama, Texas and Oklahoma , where the president has been holding rallies trying to ensure his supporters get out to vote. But in this modern era, an incendiary comment can travel fast online and leave Republicans running in competitive districts in awkward spots, trying to distance themselves from Trump .
Trump made the remarks during a rambling speech in which he said gas prices would be lower soon, touted his ouster of Venezuela’s dictator, and made attacks on news outlets.
Overall, political observers see the episode as an example of how the president’s political strategy can be unpredictable at a time when Republicans are trying to control the message the most.
“Whether you like Trump or not, he is good at getting his message out and coming up with a message that can resonate and catch fire,” said Mindy Romero, founder and director of the nonpartisan Center for Inclusive Democracy. “I think the question now is: Is he starting to fail himself when it comes to his messaging?”
California Democrats were quick to use Trump’s remarks as a line of attack against him. Gov. Gavin Newsom called him “deranged and dangerous” and opened the state emergency operations center to assess potential threats. San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria told Trump to “keep our city out of your reckless war talk.” And Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said his comments could “potentially compromise our safety.”
Trump’s remarks about the California cities on Monday were the most striking example yet of the president using California as a foil to rally  a base in GOP strongholds.
In Nebraska and other red states in recent days, Trump has repeatedly cast California as a political boogeyman as a means to motivate voters to cast their ballots for the GOP candidates.
At an Oklahoma rally last week, Trump told the crowd that Republicans need to keep the party in control of Congress so that his administration can continue the work of combating fraud in blue states, like California. The administration’s efforts, led by Vice President JD Vance, have sometimes been overestimated or nebulous.
But Trump tells supporters that in places like California, the administration is seeing “billions and billions of dollars of fraud.”
In a social media post Monday, Trump began blaming the cost of fuel — a defining issue for voters this election cycle — on states like California.
“What’s driving up Gasoline is no longer the Strait of Hormuz,” Trump wrote. The issue, he said, is refineries being “closed up in Blue States, like California, by the Dumocrats.”
Hours later, while rallying in Nebraska, Trump seemed to contradict himself as he promised the crowd that fuel costs would go down once the war in Iran was over.
“That will end very quickly, one way or the other, very soon, maybe a little after the election, maybe a little before, but it is going to end very soon,” Trump said. “When that happens, the oil will come tumbling down.”
Trump’s messaging underscores how the war with Iran, which has gas prices topping $6 a gallon, has emerged as a potential liability for Republicans that the president is trying to address in subtle ways.
Polling on Trump’s handling of the economy has remained low, even among Republicans. A University of Massachusetts Amherst poll last month found that only 22% of Americans perceive the economy in a good or fair state.
In California, a poll by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies , co-sponsored by The Times, found that 70% of California voters disapprove of Trump’s decision to go to war in Iran, including 1 in 5 Republicans.
The softening of Trump’s approval even among those who still support his performance could translate into lower GOP turnout in the state’s few competitive races, the poll’s director, Mark DiCamillo, said.
Trump’s strategy in the final stretch before the midterms has largely focused on rallying the base in hopes that they will turn out to vote. Part of that strategy includes using California as a punching bag.
One particular line of attack has been disparaging the state’s voting systems. He suggested Monday that Democrat-led cities are trying to cheat in November as he touted the fast count of ballots in foreign countries.
“In Detroit, Philadelphia, California and numerous other U.S. Cities and States, the results, with much smaller numbers, will often take weeks to Rig, I mean, calculate,” Trump wrote on Monday. “Voting in America is CORRUPT!!!”
In another social media post, he said: “California: Took 38 days with 16.1 million ballots in 2024.”’
Trump using California as a foil for any given issue could be a risky strategy, Romero said.
“He’s expanding the types of things that he’s blaming California for, like the gas crisis,” she said, arguing that such statements could “start to lose credibility with those people that he has credibility with.”
For Republican voters in California, the ploy may be even riskier, especially when Trump suggests Iran could “take out” their cities.
“I don’t think that message necessarily plays well here because Californians are Californians,” DiCamillo said. “There is a certain pride in being a Californian, certainly not held by everybody ... but I would think that the mainstream would be defending the state.”

LONDON – For decades we have lived in a world that seemed to transcend geography.
Information, money, goods, germs and weapons have come to defy distance. Whispered confidences and billion-dollar bounties are traded instantaneously. Smartphones, satsumas and sandals are delivered to your doorstep from across the globe. Ballistic missiles are able to traverse continents in minutes.
But such everyday assumptions have been challenged by the economic havoc wrought by the blockage of a single vital shipping and energy route in the Persian Gulf.

articles.title_orig: Fontaines D.C.'s decadent, dystopian vision of our time
articles.title_zh: Fontaines D.C.'s decadent, dystopian vision of our time
articles.content_orig:
"We're in a glorious age of distraction," says Grian Chatten, the lead singer of the Irish band Fontaines D.C. "I just want to make people really feel things about the world that they live in. Because it's such a terrifying world at the moment." Elizaveta Porodina hide caption
At almost exactly the midpoint of our conversation about the fifth album made by his band, Fontaines D.C. , Grian Chatten said to me, "It's an interesting time to be a self." We'd been talking about the themes on Dopamine Chamber , which comes out on Friday, Oct. 16, and could serve as a soundtrack to the era we live in now, what Chatten calls our "glorious age of distraction."
It's also an interesting time to be a rock band in the mainstream, and that's where Fontaines D.C., which formed in 2014, definitely lives these days. The Irish quintet's next tour has them in stadiums and arenas, and the one guest on Dopamine Chamber is pop's universal "it" girl, the Spanish singer Rosalía .
The 2024 album Romance took Fontaines to another level, earning them two Grammy nominations and their best sales ever, with hits like the sweet and earnest " Favourite ." Following it up, Fontaines didn't take the easy way. Instead, they explored new sounds to create a captivating sonic travelogue that somehow connects the decadent beauty of old Europe with the narcotic ethereality of cyberspace.
Things really gel for Fontaines on Dopamine Chamber . Using vintage synthesizers and studio effects, the band builds on the hypnotic energy that has always been its calling card to make something huge and seductive and haunting. I was lucky to speak with Chatten about his evolution as a storyteller and his place within a band that's always growing, but which remains utterly true to itself.
This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. You can listen to an extended version of this interview, plus a conversation with Fontaines D.C. bassist Conor Deegan, in the audio at the top of this page, or in the NPR Music podcast .
Ann Powers, NPR: This album comes at a kind of a milestone point in the career of Fontaines. You're playing these huge venues now, and emerging as a truly superstar band at this point. I don't know how you feel about that, but I wondered if the fact that your audience has grown so much influenced the direction this album went in. I mean in a very positive way that you seem to be kind of aiming for a monumental sound to connect with this new level of your career.
Grian Chatten: You know, the fact that there is an audience that has grown and continued to listen and moves with us, I certainly feel like it's a collaboration between ourselves and our audience, if you know what I mean. It's like, through each album, we're kind of getting closer in a spaceship to this black hole or something like that.
Well, I hope you don't fall down the black hole, because then I won't be able to hear your music anymore.
Maybe you'll have already heard it, years ago.
Oh my god, you're blowing my mind. On Dopamine Chamber there's this experience of displacement that you're getting at, and you sing a little bit about [immortality], the hubris of someone who thinks they might live forever. So how does this new album relate to those themes?
I feel like I'm writing about a metaphysical place or an imagined place that represents or reflects where I think we might be headed. And I want to do it with all the trappings and all the details of the things that I find affecting in my life: things that scare me about the future and things that warm me about the past, things that kind of comfort me. I like the idea that it's almost like a spectrum. You know the Italian singer Mina ? She came through in the '60s and she maintained a career for decades after, she's still alive, and I'm really in love with her music. And that informed and kind of armed the sense of humanity that I wanted to imbue this record with.
And then on the [other] end of the spectrum is kind of a darker, more industrial … dare I say the cliche word now: dystopian. That's people like John Mouse, who, I don't know if I [should] plug him, or like Depeche Mode and New Order and like Disintegration by The Cure . I wanted the record to feel like it was a distinct place where you walked through and you felt both of these things interacting with each other so that you could kind of get a sense of what we're losing and where we might be headed towards, you know?
Well, a dystopian story is only effective if there is a strong sense of humanity. I think about a film like Under the Skin . I mean, if Scarlett Johansson isn't there in her beauty, it doesn't have the same effect. You need to have that in any dystopian [setting]. You have to have that depth of emotion, and physical sensuality to counter and be in a dynamic relationship with machines. So maybe that's what you're going for?
Bjork does it. She's got such a beautiful, emotive and human voice. To have that piercing through the industrial music on, like, Homogenic , she had it sewn up there. I really like the feeling in Ridley Scott's films. You know, they might be isolated in a vacuum in space like how many thousands of miles or light years away from planet Earth, but they're still falling in love with each other and they've got a job to do, and a mission.
I [heard] something you said about your process to Jools Holland . You said you like to write on toilet paper because it has to go in the bin, which I thought was a little bit of that Irish humour, perhaps, but also the idea for a writer to say, "I want to cling to a notion of ephemerality about my own process." Does that free you up? The idea that your lyrics, your words, your poetry moves through space and might dissolve?
I think it's going to sound painfully, incredibly Irish of me but it's very it's important for me to recognize the transience of my own ideas and my own work, particularly before I kind of actually kind of cast them in stone in the recording and put it out there, you know, into the into the astral plane. You know, I think it's important to consider the fact that each thing I write is doomed or is to be forgotten unless I decide to actually sit down and do something about it. And I think what that does — I don't know if this makes sense — but what that does to me as a writer is it builds up my confidence in myself as the generator of the ideas, as opposed to kind of becoming beholden to one lucky burst of an idea.
But then, you know, you're writing about digital spaces on this record, and there's a sense of, everything lasts forever in digital space. I wonder if that was something you were thinking about.
That very concept of everything lasting forever immediately just makes me feel sick with how meaningless that renders everything. Like, things acquire their meaning because they're ephemeral. People love each other fiercely because they know that they're going to get old and die, you know?
A thread on this record is cinema, the idea of life as a movie. But also I know you're very inspired by films. Let's just talk about "Marianne" for a minute. I know it was inspired by the Netflix version of The Talented Mr. Ripley with Andrew Scott. When you watch something like that, how do you translate it into a song?
For me, often it takes me a while to process things.
It's not like I watched the first couple of episodes and started writing things down. It kind of ruminated for a while until I realized that the feelings I wanted to express, I was kind of like, "Oh yeah, that's how I felt when I was watching that thing." And then I kind of, at least emotionally, just thought about Andrew Scott's performance and that cinematography, the lingering shots of Italy and someone running away and, I suppose, trying to replace a human soul with material possessions and a life that isn't your own. For some reason [it was] profoundly resonant for me.
I feel like decadence is a theme that connects that song with its inspiration. And I think one questio

articles.title_orig: The world's hottest AI stock market has gone cold
articles.title_zh: The world's hottest AI stock market has gone cold
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
South Korea went from the world's hottest stock market to its coldest in months.
Taiwan is pulling ahead as investors broaden AI bets beyond memory chips.
Asia's AI trade is expanding from memory chips to the broader hardware supply chain.
South Korea's stock market has gone from the world's hottest to its coldest in just a few months.
The Kospi, the world's best-performing major stock benchmark in the first half of 2026, has since fallen about 24%, making it the worst-performing major market in the second half. It's still more than 50% higher this year.
The AI trade isn't losing its appeal. But investors are increasingly looking beyond South Korea's memory-chip giants to companies with broader exposure to the AI hardware boom.
In July, analysts at GlobalData.TS Lombard pointed out that much of the earnings growth at Korean memory-chip makers came from higher memory-chip prices. By contrast, TSMC and Japanese chip-equipment makers relied more on advanced manufacturing and process expertise, giving them more durable growth prospects, they added.
Taiwan's Taiex has climbed about 7% in the second half of the year, taking its year-to-date gains to about 70% as investors broaden their bets across the AI hardware supply chain.
South Korea's rally was driven largely by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, whose soaring memory-chip profits made them among the biggest winners of the AI boom. Together, the companies account for more than half of the Kospi, leaving the market unusually dependent on a single segment of the semiconductor industry.
Even blockbuster earnings are no longer enough to excite investors. Last Thursday, Samsung forecast a nearly ninefold increase in quarterly operating profit, yet its shares have fallen for two straight trading sessions.
The reversal followed months of extraordinary volatility. The Kospi plunged 22% in July, its worst month since the 2008 financial crisis, before rebounding 18% on the month's final trading day for its biggest one-day gain on record. The swings triggered multiple market-wide circuit breakers as leveraged bets on chip stocks amplified the moves.
Young South Koreans flooded social media with memes and dark humor about their battered portfolios, while regulators tightened rules on leveraged single-stock exchange-traded funds after concerns the products had fueled speculation.
Trading has cooled sharply. Turnover has dropped 70% from its late-May peak, while foreign investors have continued pulling money from Korean equities.
The shift didn't happen overnight.
Even before Korea's selloff, investors were debating whether the next phase of the AI boom would continue rewarding memory-chip makers or broaden to companies with exposure across the semiconductor supply chain.
Taiwan appears to be benefiting from that shift. Its market offers exposure across AI infrastructure, from advanced chip manufacturing and packaging to servers and networking equipment.
That includes TSMC as well as companies involved in advanced packaging, servers, networking equipment, and other AI infrastructure.
The Taiex outperformed the Kospi by more than 23 percentage points in the third quarter, as Taiwan's benchmark gained nearly 4% while South Korea's plunged more than 19%.

articles.title_orig: Preview: No Asian stars makes Santiago more open
articles.title_zh: Preview: No Asian stars makes Santiago more open
articles.content_orig:
It is one of the last major competitions of the outdoor season in para archery but arguably one of the most open.
Santiago 2026 is the penultimate stage of the inaugural Hyundai World Para Series, following on from Bangkok , Nove Mesto and Ahmedabad , with the circuit closing in Dubai in December.
However, the action in Chile's capital city promises to be one of the most open fields of the year, as all of Asia's top archers will not travel to South America due to the first day of the Asian Para Games overlapping with the individual finals on Sunday 18 October.
This includes athletes such as India's Paralympic medallists Singh Harvinder and Sheetal Devi and Singapore's Ken Swagumilang, the runner up of the Beijing 2025 Asia Para Archery Championships .
They may be big hitters in their respective categories, but what their absence does do is pave the path for some of the best para archers from the Americas to win world ranking points - where the vast majority of entries for Santiago come from - and potentially create new stars.
That still may be a tall order in the W1 men and women categories, however, as world number ones Jason Tabansky and Sarka Pultar Musilova are shooting at the Peñalolen National Training Center, as is the second-ranked Samuel Molina in the para recurve men discipline, who won stage three in Ahmedabad earlier this year.
Host nation Chile has the largest squad, with 12 total competitors, whilst countries outside of the Americas have travelled as well, including three from Musilova's Czechia and four from Romania.
What’s happening? The fourth stage of the Hyundai World Archery Para Series from 14 to 18 October at the Peñalolen National Training Center in Santiago, Chile.
What’s at stake? World ranking points.
Who’s competing? 52 archers from 10 nations.
What’s the story? No Asian archers means Santiago is one of the smallest para competitions of the year but offers the chance for the best archers in the para compound, recurve, visually impaired and W1 categories from the Americas and Europe to win world ranking points, as well as birthing new stars from those regions.

Live scores will be available on the World Archery website, with coverage across World Archery’s digital platforms throughout the competition.

articles.title_orig: Kazakhstan Receives IJF Flag Ahead of 2027 World Judo Championships
articles.title_zh: Kazakhstan Receives IJF Flag Ahead of 2027 World Judo Championships
articles.content_orig:
By Dana Omirgazy in Sports on 12 October 2026
ASTANA — Kazakhstan has officially received the International Judo Federation (IJF) flag to host the 2027 World Judo Championships in Kazakh capital on June 7-14. The event will be the country’s second time hosting the sport’s premier global competition and an important step toward the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Photo credit: Press Service of the Kazakhstan Judo Federation
The handover ceremony took place in Baku, Azerbaijan, during the World Championships. IJF Secretary General Lisa Allan presented the flag to Kuanyshbek Yessekeyev, president of the Judo Federation of Kazakhstan, following its transfer by Elnur Mammadli, vice president of the Azerbaijan Judo Federation, reported the federation’s press service on Oct. 10.
The 2027 championships will serve as an important stage in Olympic qualification, with athletes competing for ranking points toward securing places at the Los Angeles Games.
Yessekeyev said hosting the event reflects the international community’s confidence in Kazakhstan’s ability to organize major sporting competitions. He added that the federation would focus on meeting IJF organizational standards and preparing the national team for competition.
Kazakhstan first hosted the World Judo Championships in 2015. The country has also hosted the Qazaqstan Barysy Grand Slam from 2023 through 2026, an international tournament on the IJF calendar that contributes to Olympic qualification.

articles.title_orig: EU adopts nearly 1,600 new sanctions listings targeting Russia
articles.title_zh: EU adopts nearly 1,600 new sanctions listings targeting Russia
articles.content_orig:
The European Union has imposed sanctions on nearly 1,600 Russian individuals and companies linked to Russia’s arms industry
BRUSSELS -- The European Union imposed sanctions on Monday on almost 1,600 Russian people and companies linked to Russia’s arms industry, notably targeting those suspected of involvement in making parts for drones and missiles.
In the biggest single listing of sanctions since the Kremlin launched full-scale war on Ukraine almost five years ago, the EU also targeted 77 people accused of organizing, working on, or running in “sham elections” in occupied parts of Ukraine.
Announcing the sanctions, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said that more than half of them “address the production chain for the ballistic missiles Russia uses to kill Ukrainian civilians every day.”
“This is not the time to ease pressure on Moscow but to increase it,” she said.
The EU said the companies are on a list established by the Russian government itself “that identifies them as belonging to the Russian military-industrial complex, and they are therefore entitled to receive subsidies.”
The EU considers those officials running the companies to be “supporting Russia’s military and industrial complex.” It said the sanctions are aimed at “mid-level suppliers that represent the ‘core’ of the Russian military industry.”
The components they provide include electronics, communication equipment, radar and navigation systems, satellite and missile systems, as well as explosives and ammunition.
The move brings the total number of Russian officials and “entities” targeted by the EU to more than 4,500, including President Vladimir Putin, oligarchs suspected of backing him and scores of lawmakers, as well as banks and the shadow fleet illicitly shipping oil.

articles.title_orig: World Bank jobs council urges 'crisis-era' employment support measures as IMF warns of AI ‘tsunami’
articles.title_zh: World Bank jobs council urges 'crisis-era' employment support measures as IMF warns of AI ‘tsunami’
articles.content_orig:
BANGKOK — Policymakers are moving from debating whether artificial intelligence will hit jobs to issuing stark warnings about AI-led disruption and recommending measures on cushioning the fallout.
International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Monday that artificial intelligence was hitting the global labor market like a "slow-moving tsunami," with young graduates first in line to be knocked down.
"People to worry about, first and foremost, [are] young people that are coming into the labor market," Georgieva said at a panels on Monday. "Normally, they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then grow up the ranks. But if they're gone, I don't think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as ... professional future."
Speaking on the same panel, Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, who co-chairs the World Bank's Jobs Council, called for governments to make "crisis-era" support measures a permanent tool for getting young people into work.
What governments did during the Covid-19 pandemic and, in some cases, the global financial crisis "now has to be thought of not as a crisis measure, but as part of the structural, the menu of structural policies," he said.
That means working with the private sector, and incentivizing firms to hire fresh graduates, because "the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand," Shanmugaratnam said.
The remarks show that policymakers are moving from debating whether AI will disrupt jobs to deciding how to cushion the fallout, at a time when rapidly aging populations, particularly in Asia, already threaten to shrink workforces.
World Bank President Ajay Banga, estimates 1.2 billion young people will turn 18 over the next 15 years, and the private sector, which already generates 75% to 85% of jobs in any country, will have to absorb most of them.
Governments' role is to make that possible, he said, by building infrastructure, setting policy and "de-risking" private capital, or lowering the risks that deter investors from putting in money at scale. "It is private capital that creates jobs," he said.
The IMF estimates that about 40% of jobs worldwide will eventually be "augmented, downgraded or eliminated." Exposure is about 60% in advanced economies and 23% in low-income countries, she said, but poorer nations are not better off: that is "just because AI is further away."
The squeeze is clearest in tech, Shanmugaratnam said, adding that in the U.S. "for the first time in a century, demand for graduates has gone down," with the wage premium for a college degree also shrinking. Without action, a cohort of graduates loses more than a year of skills: "you lose trust in the future," he said.
AI has also been the major driver propping up growth this year. AI-related investments and trade have lifted output in a handful of economies, helping keep global expansion near 3% despite an energy supply shock, Georgieva said.
"Love it, hate it, or fear it. It [AI] is here, and we are already seeing the first wave of impact," Georgieva said, estimating AI adoption could lift growth by 0.5 percentage point to 1 percentage point in advanced Asia, and 0.2 percentage point to 0.8 percentage point in emerging Asia. At the high end, that "would more than offset the loss that comes from aging population," said Georgieva.
Shanmugaratnam cautioned that growth alone may not necessarily deliver job creation. China, India and developing Southeast Asia are "growing quite well, but job creation is weak," he said, and AI "is going to widen that divergence if we are too passive about it."
AI-induced job displacement, however, will come "task by task," he said, "and that gives us time" — provided workers can learn on the job and universities shift toward applied training.

articles.title_orig: Nations of the world have forgotten responsibility toward the less privileged
articles.title_zh: Nations of the world have forgotten responsibility toward the less privileged
articles.content_orig:
Children are served their school meal at a school in India in this 2017 photograph. (OSV News/Courtesy Mary's Meals)
The glory of God is being fully alive; this has given us the impetus to live life to the fullest. The changing face of the universe has impacted the responses of us humans, maybe for the worst. Though to be honest a few good people do struggle to keep alive some values which are so essential for the coexistence of all living organisms.
There was a time when we experienced interdependency and we happily lived by it. Over the years what has been frightening is the role of power in our lives. Instead of being facilitators we have become owners, holders of power — the remote control lies in the powerful.
Nations of the world have forgotten their responsibility toward the less privileged.
The Global North and Global South are socioeconomic and political classifications, not strict geographic ones. The North includes wealthy, developed nations (U.S., Europe, Japan, Australia), while the South encompasses developing regions (Africa, Latin America and most of Asia). The South holds roughly 85% of the world's population but only accounts for about 40% of the global GDP.
The Global North and the Global South are often defined in terms of their differing levels of wealth, economic development, income inequality and strength of democracy, as well as by their political freedom and economic freedom, as defined by a variety of indices. Countries of the Global North tend to be wealthier, and export technologically advanced manufactured products, among other characteristics.
In contrast, countries of the Global South tend to be relatively poorer, and heavily dependent on their largely agrarian-based economic primary sectors. Some scholars suggest that the inequality gap between the Global North and the Global South has narrowed since globalization. Others contend that the Global South has instead become poorer vis-à-vis the Global North.
According to this data there is an urgent question which we need to ask: Who then is responsible for this lopsided development? Due to longstanding wars with the Middle East, the Global North is drastically cutting funds for the welfare of poorer nations. This is going to affect the Global South in a very serious manner. The poorer nations will be denied welfare services that were being carried out by the nongovernmental sector.
Being in the social sector, I hear many painful stories of retrenchment of staff, as funds are not available. What has shocked me most is the cutting of staff at the U.N. office here in Patna-Bihar. So many of the agreements which have been signed by countries will no longer stand valid. In other words, who will we question? The global world is becoming less accountable. We are losing our ethos as nations who once reached out as a moral responsibility to the less privileged.
What is more frightening is what I hear — people who have worked in this sector in big international agencies for three decades saying what's next. One said: "I can't sleep at night. I have a young family. What's their future? I am in midlife now, I can't all of a sudden change my profession. Where will I get a job? How will I become self-employed?"
This is a nightmare for many of the youth of our country. India being a young nation, unemployment being high, industries being insufficient, basic necessities of life are going beyond the reach of the common person. In this present scenario, I am asking myself, do we have a role to play?
Vulnerability is on the increase, life is becoming fragile. The question before us is how will we differentiate; what will we prioritize and at what cost? These are soul-searching questions each human person has to face every day. When peace of mind is not possible, when one is weighed down with heavy burdens — how does one live? The big question today is, are we moving backward? Has development in the real sense of the word affected us?
The fragility of security seems to have become a privilege of a very few, those in administrative services or political parties. These are the ones who make decisions which will affect the whole of humanity into the future.
I am reminded of the talisman of Mahatma Gandhi:
Whenever you are in doubt or when the self becomes too much with you, apply the following test. Recall the face of the poorest and the weakest man whom you may have seen and ask yourself, if the step you contemplate is going to be of any use to him. Will he gain anything by it? Will it restore him to a control over his own life and destiny? In other words, will it lead to swaraj [freedom] for the hungry and spiritually starving millions? Then you will find your doubts and your self melting away.

articles.title_orig: Opensignal Launches World’s First Interactive Map of Satellite-to-Smartphone D2D Connections
articles.title_zh: Opensignal Launches World’s First Interactive Map of Satellite-to-Smartphone D2D Connections
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Provides Independent, Real-World Global View of Direct-to-Device Activity
BOSTON, October 12, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )--Opensignal, a global independent consumer connectivity analytics and insights company, today launched the Opensignal D2D Satellite Map , the world's first interactive, real-world depiction of where direct-to-device (D2D) satellite connections with smartphones are happening across the globe. Every point on the map, which will be updated monthly, represents a location where smartphones have connected to a D2D service since January 2026, extracted from Opensignal's billions of real-world measurements.
"D2D is reshaping who can deliver mobile coverage, and where, because the phone in your pocket can now reach a satellite directly. Until now, the industry has had to make decisions without knowing where momentum and adoption are real," said Mike Sandy, President, Market Performance at Opensignal. "The Opensignal D2D Satellite Map provides an independent view of where D2D is taking hold across the globe, so decisions about partnerships, spectrum and devices can be grounded in how consumers are actually connecting today. As D2D matures, that view will only become more important."
While satellite broadband is a well-established offering for home and business internet, D2D is a newer, rapidly growing area. Many of today's standard smartphones can now connect directly to satellites, extending mobile coverage to places terrestrial networks don't, or can't, reach. As of August 2026, the Global mobile Suppliers Association (GSA) reports that 23 partnerships have launched satellite-to-cellphone services.
Current D2D services are largely limited to text messaging, emergency alerts and a small set of apps, constrained by limited spectrum, early-generation satellite and handset hardware, and standards that are still evolving. Mobile operators and satellite companies are working toward enabling voice and higher-speed data, while regulators are weighing how to make more spectrum available for D2D. In addition to where connections are happening, Opensignal expects to show how well these connections perform as D2D services mature, similar to its mobile network experience analyses.
You can find the Opensignal D2D Satellite Map at https://d2d.opensignal.com .
Opensignal is a global independent consumer connectivity analytics and insights company, delivering an unmatched combination of real-world network data and competitive market intelligence. Its insights are fueled by 50+ billion daily data points from over 100 million devices worldwide on mobile, fixed broadband, and satellite networks, alongside pricing, promotions, and competitive conditions, showing how consumers actually experience connectivity and why they switch. In addition to public network benchmark reports and market insights, Opensignal delivers this intelligence through its portfolio of premium solutions, including Opensignal Network Experience Suite, Opensignal Subscriber Analytics, Frontline Network Experience, and GeoResults. Headquartered in Boston, Opensignal has offices in Canada, the UK, Poland and Singapore. For more information, visit https://opensignal.com .

articles.title_orig: Bishops around the world ask for prayers for Pope Leo XIV’s health
articles.title_zh: Bishops around the world ask for prayers for Pope Leo XIV’s health
articles.content_orig:
Prayers for the pope’s health have been pouring in from all over the world.
Bishops from around the world asked for prayers for Pope Leo XIV after he announced on Sunday, Oct. 11, that he will undergo surgery to remove a nodule on one of his lungs in the coming days.
In the United States, Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the U.S. bishops’ conference, said the prelates would join “the faithful and all people of good will in praying for his good health.” He also prayed for those who will perform the operation: “May the hand of Pope Leo’s surgeons be guided by the divine physician, Jesus Christ.”
Archbishop Ronald Hicks of New York joined the prayers as he finished a week-long pilgrimage on the Camino de Santiago in Spain. “I join with the bishops, priests, faithful, and all people of good will of the Archdiocese of New York in praying for our Holy Father, Pope Leo XIV, as he prepares for his surgery later this week,” he wrote . He also asked Jesus, “the divine physician,” to care for the pope and guide “the hands of his surgeons, nurses, and other health professionals.”
Cardinal Daniel Sturla, archbishop of Montevideo, also wrote about the news. Uruguay is one of the countries expecting Pope Leo XIV on his upcoming visit to Latin America. “Let us pray for his speedy recovery and continue with greater spirit the preparation for his visit to our land,” he wrote.
In Peru, which also expects the pope later this year, the Archdiocese of Lima entrusted his health to the Lord of Miracles, a devotion that draws millions of Peruvians each year. “We ask the Lord of Miracles for his speedy recovery,” the archdiocese said on social media.
The Peruvian bishops’ conference issued a message titled “United in prayer for the health of the Holy Father Leo XIV.” It noted the :serenity and humility” with which the pope shared the news and asked that his health be entrusted to the Lord of Miracles.
“Lifting to God, Lord of life and source of all health, our supplications that he strengthen him and grant him the health that the fulfillment of his mission requires,” the Peruvian bishops said. They also urged communities, families, and the faithful to place the Holy Father under the maternal protection of the Blessed Virgin Mary, so that in the fullness of his strength he may continue his mission in service of the Church and all humanity, as a messenger of peace and hope and a witness of unity, fraternity, and encounter among all peoples.
The Argentinian bishops said in a statement: “We ask the Lord to grant him strength and peace at this time, that the operation may go well, and that he may make a swift and full recovery.”
The Spanish bishops’ conference also invited prayer for the pope. Its president, Archbishop Luis Argüello, asked “the whole Spanish Church — dioceses, institutes of consecrated life, communities and lay associations, all members of the People of God, and our fellow citizens — to pray for the health of our beloved Pope Leo XIV.”
The conference’s secretary general, Bishop Francisco César García Magán, recalled the welcome Leo XIV received on his recent visit to Spain and said the faithful can now show him their closeness in another way: “Now we show it by uniting in prayer.”
The conference’s secretary general, Bishop Francisco César García Magán, recalled the welcome Leo XIV received on his recent visit to Spain and said the faithful can now show him their closeness in another way: “Now we show it by uniting in prayer.”
Archbishop Tadeusz Wojda, the president of the Polish Bishops’ Conference, issued an appeal to the Polish people, asking them to “pray for the Holy Father, Pope Leo XIV, asking God for a successful operation and a speedy recovery.”
Bishop John Keenan, on behalf of the Scottish bishops’ conference, said : “We invite Catholics across Scotland, and all people of goodwill, to join us in praying for Pope Leo, for the medical team caring for him, and for a successful operation and a full and speedy recovery.”
Archbishop Richard Moth of Westminster and the president of the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of England and Wales, assured Leo of the prayers of the faithful.
“We pray that following the procedure and a period of recovery, he will soon be restored to health,” Moth wrote.
Archbishop Charles Scicluna, Archbishop of Malta and Adjunct Secretary of the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, wrote on X : “The Church in Malta is united in prayer for the Holy Father, wishing him well for the surgery he will be undergoing.”
The pope announced the operation after Sunday’s Angelus. Doctors found a nodule on one of his lungs and recommended removing it. In sharing the news, Leo asked the faithful to accompany him spiritually in the coming days: “I entrust myself to your prayer.”

articles.title_orig: North Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles towards the sea
articles.title_zh: North Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles towards the sea
articles.content_orig:
North Korea has fired multiple ballistic missiles towards the sea off its east coast, South Korea’s military says.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said one of the missiles launched from the Pyongyang area flew more than 900km (559 miles) on Monday. The joint chiefs did not specify how many missiles were detected.
Japan’s Deputy Defence Minister Takashi Koyari said at least two missiles were launched 17 minutes apart and landed in waters outside of its exclusive economic zone.
Koyari said the first missile flew about 220 kilometres (137 miles) and the second more than 910 kilometres (565 miles), following an “irregular” flight path and suggested it may have been a hypersonic weapon.
South Korea’s presidential office said that Pyongyang’s repeated missile launches violate United Nations Security Council resolutions, urging an immediate stop.
Monday’s launches add to heightened tensions on the Korean Peninsula, as both countries have been conducting weapons tests.
JCS spokesperson Jang Do-young said the latest missile launch appears to be a show of force, days after South Korea tested its own hypersonic weapon.
On Thursday, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung oversaw the country’s first test-firing of a hypersonic missile, a rare public showcasing of a missile test by a South Korean president.
Lee’s office said the hypersonic weapon, once fully developed, would enhance South Korea’s ability to strike key targets by surprise in the “Korean Peninsula theatre of operations”.
On October 3, North Korea also tested a hypersonic intermediate-range missile designed to evade missile defences in South Korea and Japan.
Last week, Seoul demanded an apology after a landmine blast wounded three soldiers in the Demilitarized Zone between South and North Korea. A joint South Korean-UN investigation concluded that two landmines were planted by North Korean forces about a year ago. Pyongyang dismissed the claim and accused South Korea of provocation.
Prior to the border mine blast, Seoul said it was conducting “preliminary coordination efforts” to facilitate dialogue between Pyongyang and Washington.
Lee pledged to reopen dialogue with North Korea in his first speech after taking office in 2025.
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un continues to flaunt his nuclear weapons programme, while rejecting US and South Korean offers to resume stalled diplomacy.
Talks between Kim and United States President Donald Trump abruptly ended in 2019. Kim Jong Un’s government continues to demand that Washington abandon its “hostile” policy towards Pyongyang and drop demands for North Korea’s denuclearisation as a condition for talks.

Pathos Communications Plc (LSE:NEWS) will sponsor the World Media Congress 2026 in Madrid and present to attendees.
Its sponsorship covers the board and VIP lunch at the event, organised by the publishing industry network FIPP, which is part of WAN-IFRA.

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Simon nears Mexico with 155 mph winds and flooding fears
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Simon nears Mexico with 155 mph winds and flooding fears
articles.content_orig:
Workers place sandbags outside a restaurant as Hurricane Simon approaches Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. Fernando Llano/AP hide caption
PUERTO VALLARTA, Mexico — Hurricane Simon pounded Mexico's Pacific coast as a Category 3 storm on Sunday, its eye remaining just offshore as its most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre and the ocean.
The hurricane's center swirled parallel to the coast, closing in on the Puerto Vallarta area, where its most damaging winds and rain were expected to hit around midnight and continue through Monday morning. Its maximum sustained winds weakened Sunday to 120 mph (195 kph), according to the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami, but it was still expected to remain a dangerous hurricane.
That's not good news for people in and around Puerto Vallarta, a popular tourist destination in the state of Jalisco. Just inland and uphill from the resort areas, many Mexicans live in communities where housing might not stand up to the storm.
By Sunday afternoon, Simon's eye was moving northwest about 45 miles (75 kilometers) south of Cabo Corrientes at about 5 mph (7 kph). A senior hurricane center specialist, Philippe Papin, said this westernmost tip of mainland Mexico is the area most likely to get a direct hit from the system. Cabo Corrientes is at the southern tip of Bahia de Banderas, the wide bay where Puerto Vallarta looks out to the Pacific.
Hurricane-force winds extend outward up to 15 miles (30 kilometers), and tropical-storm-force winds reach up to 60 miles (95 kilometers) from Simon's center, meaning the entire area between Mexico's western coast and the Sierra Madre mountains could be affected.
"We're expecting catastrophic wind and life-threatening storm surge impacts along that west-central coast of Mexico where the hurricane warning is currently in effect," Papin said. "They're also getting very heavy rainfall associated with the storm that's likely going to produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides in areas of higher terrain along the Mexican coastline, and there will be significant swells."
The hurricane center on Sunday said Simon was expected to dump an additional 2 to 4 inches (5 to 10 centimeters) of rain, with some areas getting up to 8 inches (20 centimeters), in the states of Colima, Jalisco, Nayarit and Sinaloa through early Thursday.
"Isolated maximum storm totals of 30 inches (76 centimeters) are possible over portions of the states of Michoacan, Colima, and Jalisco," the center said in its latest advisory. "This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides or worsen any on-going flooding, especially in areas of steep terrain."
As the storm approached Puerto Vallarta, National Guard vehicles patrolled the streets while police used a megaphone to call out the few people who were jogging, walking their dogs or biking by the waterfront. Officers reminded people that the area was closed and urged them to take shelter. Not everyone followed the orders.
Jalisco state suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating people from at-risk areas while asking the tourism sector to make sure workers and visitors are fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum took to the social platform X on Sunday to urge people in Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit and Michoacan to stay sheltered until the government issues a notification that the danger has passed. She also asked people to follow recommendations from civil protection officials and to avoid traveling on public roads.
"Precautionary evacuation efforts to safe zones are ongoing; the priority is our safety," she wrote.
A National Guard stands in the spray as a wave hits the seawall brought by the approaching Hurricane Simon in Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026. Fernando Llano/AP hide caption
Hotel worker Víctor Martínez went shopping for nonperishable food Sunday afternoon. He said he could not go to work because public transportation service was suspended and most of the hotel had been evacuated.
Martínez found people's concerns about the hurricane comforting.
"It happened to us before. It hit us years ago," Martínez said, referring to a Category 5 hurricane that hit the area in 2002. "People didn't expect it. We were very skeptical that it would ever hit us. Now, though, we're different. Precautions are being taken. It happened to us once, and we won't let it happen again."
Despite the risks posed by Simon, tourists were still arriving in Puerto Vallarta.
Visitors Ricardo Ramírez and Brenda Villarreal, who have never lived through a hurricane, went looking for food by the city's boardwalk and came across police urging people to take shelter. Ramírez said they were completely unprepared for the situation.
"The boardwalk is closed. Be responsible. Understand!" police told passersby using a megaphone.
Ramírez said he and Villarreal had planned their four-day vacation since last year and traveled from Guadalajara, Jalisco's capital.
"We don't know the extent of the danger yet," Villarreal said. "We're just starting to see what's going on."
